name: Acc.recC_intro
description: This tool provides a way to prove that a recursive predicate holds for a given element using the recursive definition. It leverages the fact that if you have a recursive definition of a predicate and proof that it holds for an element, then a proof can be constructed by induction on the proof.
conditions: A recursive definition of the predicate 'motive' for a type α
A proof that 'motive' holds for an element 'a' of type α
conclusions: A proof that 'motive' holds for 'a' using the recursive definition
function_body: theorem recC_intro {motive : (a : α) → Acc r a → Sort v} (intro : (x : α) → (h : ∀ (y : α), r y x → Acc r y) → ((y : α) → (hr : r y x) → motive y (h y hr)) → motive x (intro x h)) {a : α} (h : ∀ (y : α), r y a → Acc r y) : recC intro (Acc.intro _ h) = intro a h (fun y hr => recC intro (h y hr)) := rfl

name: Acc.rec_eq_recC
description: A tool to demonstrate the equivalence of the Acc.rec and Acc.recC functions in Lean4.
conditions: α is a type, r is a relation on α, and motive is a family of types indexed by well-founded recursion on r.
intro, a, and t are inputs satisfying the structure expected by the induction on the accessibility predicate (Acc).
function_body: theorem rec_eq_recC : @Acc.rec = @Acc.recC := by funext α r motive intro a t induction t with | intro x h ih => dsimp only [recC_intro intro h] congr; funext y hr; exact ih _ hr

name: Acc.ndrec_eq_ndrecC
description: This tool verifies the definitional equality of the accessibility predicates Acc.ndrec and Acc.ndrecC by unfolding their definitions.
conditions: Given a type α and a relation r on α
Given a motive for proving accessibility predicates
conclusions: The accessibility predicates Acc.ndrec and Acc.ndrecC are definitionally equal
function_body:
theorem ndrec_eq_ndrecC : @Acc.ndrec = @Acc.ndrecC := by
  funext α r motive intro a t
  rw [Acc.ndrec, rec_eq_recC, Acc.ndrecC]

name: Acc.ndrecOn_eq_ndrecOnC
description: This tool demonstrates the equivalence of two definitions, `Acc.ndrecOn` and `Acc.ndrecOnC`, in Lean's dependent type theory framework.
conditions: For any predicate r on α.
conclusions: The definition of `Acc.ndrecOn` is equivalent to `Acc.ndrecOnC`.
function_body: theorem ndrecOn_eq_ndrecOnC : @Acc.ndrecOn = @Acc.ndrecOnC := by funext α r motive intro a t rw [Acc.ndrecOn, rec_eq_recC, Acc.ndrecOnC]

name: WellFounded.fixF_eq_fixFC
description: This tool proves the equality of the functions 'fixF' and 'fixFC' under the assumption that their types are the same, and by using their respective definitions and properties.
conditions: fixF and fixFC have the same type
fixF and fixFC are defined using Acc.recC and Acc.rec respectively
function_body:
theorem fixF_eq_fixFC : @fixF = @fixFC := by
  funext α r C F x a
  rw [fixF, Acc.rec_eq_recC, fixFC]

name: WellFounded.fix_eq_fixC
description: A tool that establishes the equivalence between the fixed point combinator 'fix' and the fixed point combinator 'fixC' defined using a choice function.
conditions: Existence of a fixed point combinator 'fix' defined by fix f = f (fix f).
Existence of a fixed point combinator 'fixC' defined using a choice function 'C' by fixC f = (C ∘ f) ∘ f.
conclusions: The fixed point combinators 'fix' and 'fixC' are equivalent.
function_body:
theorem fix_eq_fixC : @fix = @fixC := by
  funext α C r hwf F x
  rw [fix, fixF_eq_fixFC, fixC]

name: Std.Tactic.Ext.$extName
description: This tool provides a tactic for extensionality proofs on a given structure by automatic induction and equational reasoning.
conditions: The structure is described by a flat extensional type $ext_type
conclusions: The extensional type of the flat structure is equal to the structure itself
function_body:
theorem $extName:ident : ext_type% $flat $struct:ident :=
      fun {..} {..} => by intros; subst_eqs; rfl

name: Std.Tactic.Ext.$extIffName
description: This tool demonstrates the equivalence between two logical statements: (1) P implies Q for all x and (2) not Q implies not P for all x.
conditions: For all `x`, if `P` holds for `x` then `Q` also holds for `x`.
For all `x`, if `not Q` holds for `x` then `not P` also holds for `x`.
function_body:
theorem $extIffName:ident : ext_iff_type% $flat $struct:ident :=
  fun {..} {..} =>
    ⟨fun h => by cases h; split_ands <;> rfl,
     fun _ => by (repeat cases ‹_ ∧ _›); subst_eqs; rfl⟩

name: PUnit.ext
description: This tool proves that any two points in the unit interval are equal by matching and simplifying their values.
conditions: x and y are points in the unit interval
function_body: theorem PUnit.ext (x y : PUnit) : x = y := rfl

name: Unit.ext
description: A theorem that proves every pair of unit elements in a type is equal.
conditions: x is an element of type Unit
y is an element of type Unit
function_body: theorem Unit.ext (x y : Unit) : x = y := rfl

name: Not.intro
description: This tool defines logical negation in Lean4 using implication to False and proves that negation ¬a is equivalent to a → False.
conditions: h is a proof that a implies False (a → False)
function_body: theorem Not.intro {a : Prop} (h : a → False) : ¬a := h

name: Not.imp
description: This tool proves that if we know ¬B and A → B, then we can conclude ¬A.
function_body: theorem Not.imp {a b : Prop} (H2 : ¬b) (H1 : a → b) : ¬a := mt H1 H2

name: not_congr
description: A tool that proves the negation congruence theorem, stating that if two statements are equivalent, then their negations are also equivalent.
conclusions: the negation of a is equivalent to the negation of b
function_body: theorem not_congr (h : a ↔ b) : ¬a ↔ ¬b := ⟨mt h.2, mt h.1⟩

name: not_not_not
description: A logical tool that proves the equivalence between 'not not not a' and 'not a' for any proposition a.
function_body: theorem not_not_not : ¬¬¬a ↔ ¬a := ⟨mt not_not_intro, not_not_intro⟩

name: not_not_of_not_imp
description: This tool provides a proof that if the implication a → b is false, then the negation of the negation of a, ¬¬a, is true.
function_body: theorem not_not_of_not_imp : ¬(a → b) → ¬¬a := mt Not.elim

name: not_of_not_imp
description: A tool that asserts if a does not imply b, then b is false.
function_body: theorem not_of_not_imp {a : Prop} : ¬(a → b) → ¬b := mt fun h _ => h

name: imp_not_self
description: This theorem states that the implication of a statement leading to its negation is logically equivalent to the negation of the statement itself.
function_body: theorem imp_not_self : (a → ¬a) ↔ ¬a := ⟨fun h ha => h ha ha, fun h _ => h⟩

name: iff_def
description: This tool encapsulates the definition of logical equivalence (if and only if, ↔) of two propositions, which states that two propositions are equivalent if each one implies the other.
function_body: theorem iff_def : (a ↔ b) ↔ (a → b) ∧ (b → a) := iff_iff_implies_and_implies

name: iff_def'
description: This tool verifies the logical equivalence between the propositions: a if and only if b, if b then a, and if a then b by showing that each implies the other.
function_body: theorem iff_def' : (a ↔ b) ↔ (b → a) ∧ (a → b) := iff_def.trans And.comm

name: Eq.to_iff
description: A tool that confirms logical equivalence between two statements when they are equal.
function_body: theorem Eq.to_iff : a = b → (a ↔ b) | rfl => Iff.rfl

name: iff_of_eq
description: This tool proves that if two propositions a and b are equal, then they are logically equivalent (if and only if).
function_body: theorem iff_of_eq : a = b → (a ↔ b) := Eq.to_iff

name: neq_of_not_iff
description: A tool that shows if two statements a and b are not logically equivalent, then a is not equal to b.
conditions: Statements a and b are not logically equivalent (¬(a ↔ b))
conclusions: a is not equal to b (a ≠ b)
function_body: theorem neq_of_not_iff : ¬(a ↔ b) → a ≠ b := mt Eq.to_iff

name: iff_iff_eq
description: This tool encapsulates the equivalence of the biconditional statement (a ↔ b) and the equality statement (a = b).
conditions: a and b are propositional variables
conclusions: a ↔ b if and only if a = b
function_body: theorem iff_iff_eq : (a ↔ b) ↔ a = b := ⟨propext, iff_of_eq⟩

name: eq_iff_iff
description: A tool that encapsulates the equivalence between equality and bi-conditional for propositions.
conditions: p = q if p implies q and q implies p
p ↔ q if p implies q and q implies p
conclusions: p = q if and only if p ↔ q
function_body: theorem eq_iff_iff {p q : Prop} : (p = q) ↔ (p ↔ q) := iff_iff_eq.symm

name: of_iff_true
description: Given an equivalence between a proposition and the constant True, this tool proves that the proposition must be True.
conditions: The proposition a is equivalent to True (a ↔ True)
function_body: theorem of_iff_true (h : a ↔ True) : a := h.2 ⟨⟩

name: not_of_iff_false
description: Given the falsity of an implication "if P then Q", determine that P must also be false.
conditions: If 'if P then Q' is false
function_body: theorem not_of_iff_false : (P → Q) = False → ¬P := λ h, λ p, h (⟨p, _⟩)

name: iff_of_true
description: This tool proves that if both a and b are true, then a is equivalent to b.
function_body: theorem iff_of_true (ha : a) (hb : b) : a ↔ b := ⟨fun _ => hb, fun _ => ha⟩

name: iff_of_false
description: This tool proves that two propositions are equivalent if both are false.
function_body: theorem iff_of_false (ha : ¬a) (hb : ¬b) : a ↔ b := ⟨ha.elim, hb.elim⟩

name: iff_true_left
description: A tool proving that if a is true, then (a if and only if b) is equivalent to b.
conclusions: (a if and only if b) is equivalent to b
function_body: theorem iff_true_left (ha : a) : (a ↔ b) ↔ b := ⟨fun h => h.1 ha, iff_of_true ha⟩

name: iff_true_right
description: Proves the logical equivalence `(b ↔ a) ↔ b` for any proposition `a`.
function_body: theorem iff_true_right (ha : a) : (b ↔ a) ↔ b := Iff.comm.trans (iff_true_left ha)

name: iff_false_left
description: This tool proves that if we have ¬a, then the logical equivalence a ↔ b is equivalent to ¬b.
function_body: theorem iff_false_left (ha : ¬a) : (a ↔ b) ↔ ¬b := ⟨fun h => mt h.2 ha, iff_of_false ha⟩

name: iff_false_right
description: This theorem states that for all propositions a and b, if a is false, then (a ↔ b) is equivalent to ¬b.
function_body: theorem iff_false_right (ha : ¬a) : (b ↔ a) ↔ ¬b := Iff.comm.trans (iff_false_left ha)

name: iff_true_intro
description: This tool provides a formal method to prove that if a proposition is true, then it is equivalent to True.
function_body: theorem iff_true_intro (h : a) : a ↔ True := iff_of_true h ⟨⟩

name: iff_false_intro
description: This tool proves that if ¬a is true, then a is logically equivalent to False.
function_body: theorem iff_false_intro (h : ¬a) : a ↔ False := iff_of_false h id

name: not_iff_false_intro
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem proving that if a proposition a is true, then not a is equivalent to false.
conclusions: not a is equivalent to false
function_body: theorem not_iff_false_intro (h : a) : ¬a ↔ False := iff_false_intro (not_not_intro h)

name: iff_congr
description: A theorem tool that establishes the equivalence between two pairs of logical statements implying that all statements are pairwise equivalent.
function_body:
theorem iff_congr (h₁ : a ↔ c) (h₂ : b ↔ d) : (a ↔ b) ↔ (c ↔ d) :=
  ⟨fun h => h₁.symm.trans <| h.trans h₂, fun h => h₁.trans <| h.trans h₂.symm⟩

name: not_true
description: This tool establishes that the negation of True is logically equivalent to False.
function_body: theorem not_true : (¬True) ↔ False := iff_false_intro (not_not_intro ⟨⟩)

name: not_false_iff
description: This tool proves that double negation of False is equivalent to True using logical equivalences.
function_body: theorem not_false_iff : (¬False) ↔ True := iff_true_intro not_false

name: ne_self_iff_false
description: This theorem states that a number is not equal to itself if and only if False. It leverages the principle that any proposition P is equivalent to False if and only if its negation ¬P is true.
conclusions: For any element a, the statement a ≠ a is equivalent to False
function_body: theorem ne_self_iff_false (a : α) : a ≠ a ↔ False := not_iff_false_intro rfl

name: eq_self_iff_true
description: This tool proves that any element is equal to itself if and only if True is true.
function_body: theorem eq_self_iff_true (a : α) : a = a ↔ True := iff_true_intro rfl

name: heq_self_iff_true
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem that any element of type α is equal to itself if and only if True.
conclusions: a is equal to itself if and only if True
function_body: theorem heq_self_iff_true (a : α) : HEq a a ↔ True := iff_true_intro HEq.rfl

name: iff_not_self
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem that a proposition cannot be equivalent to its negation, establishing that ¬(P ↔ ¬P).
function_body: theorem iff_not_self : ¬(a ↔ ¬a) | H => let f h := H.1 h h; f (H.2 f)

name: not_iff_self
description: This theorem proves that the statement 'not a is equivalent to a' is false.
conditions: a valid logical system where ¬ represents negation and ↔ represents logical equivalence
function_body: theorem not_iff_self : ¬(¬a ↔ a) | H => iff_not_self H.symm

name: true_iff_false
description: This tool determines the logical equivalence of True if and only if False being equivalent to False.
conditions: True if and only if False
False if and only if False
function_body: theorem true_iff_false : (True ↔ False) ↔ False := iff_false_intro (fun h => h.1 ⟨⟩)

name: false_iff_true
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem that the biconditional of False and True is equivalent to False.
conditions: The statement False is always false.
The statement True is always true.
function_body: theorem false_iff_true : (False ↔ True) ↔ False := iff_false_intro (fun h => h.2 ⟨⟩)

name: false_of_true_iff_false
description: A theorem that states if True is equivalent to False, then False must be true.
function_body: theorem false_of_true_iff_false : (True ↔ False) → False := fun h => h.1 ⟨⟩

name: false_of_true_eq_false
description: This tool demonstrates that assuming True equals False leads to a contradiction, therefore invalidating the assumption.
function_body: theorem false_of_true_eq_false : (True = False) → False := fun h => h ▸ trivial

name: true_eq_false_of_false
description: This tool proves that 'True = False' can be derived if 'False' is provable.
function_body: theorem true_eq_false_of_false : False → (True = False) := False.elim

name: eq_comm
description: A theorem that establishes the commutativity of the equality relation.
function_body: theorem eq_comm {a b : α} : a = b ↔ b = a := ⟨Eq.symm, Eq.symm⟩

name: imp_intro
description: A tool that formalizes the theorem stating if α and β are propositions and α is true, then α implies β.
function_body: theorem imp_intro {α β : Prop} (h : α) : β → α := fun _ => h

name: imp_imp_imp
description: This tool proves that given the implications P -> Q, Q -> R, and R -> S, we can conclude P -> S.
function_body:
theorem imp_imp_imp {P Q R S : Prop} (hPQ : P -> Q) (hQR : Q -> R) (hRS : R -> S) : P -> S :=
  assume hP : P,
  show S, from hRS (hQR (hPQ hP))

name: imp_iff_right
description: This tool establishes the equivalence between the implications (a → b) and ((a → b) → b), which effectively means that for a given proposition b, if a holds, then a → b holds if and only if b holds.
conclusions: (a → b) is true if and only if b is true
function_body: theorem imp_iff_right {a : Prop} (ha : a) : (a → b) ↔ b := ⟨fun f => f ha, imp_intro⟩

name: imp_true_iff
description: A tool that proves the equivalence between the type α → True and True for any type α.
conclusions: The type α → True is equivalent to True
function_body: theorem imp_true_iff (α : Sort u) : (α → True) ↔ True := iff_true_intro fun _ => trivial

name: false_imp_iff
description: This tool proves the equivalence between the implication from a falsehood to any proposition and true.
function_body: theorem false_imp_iff (a : Prop) : (False → a) ↔ True := iff_true_intro False.elim

name: true_imp_iff
description: A tool that demonstrates the logical equivalence of 'if True, then α' being just α.
conclusions: 'if True, then α' is logically equivalent to α
function_body: theorem true_imp_iff (α : Prop) : (True → α) ↔ α := ⟨fun h => h trivial, fun h _ => h⟩

name: imp_self
description: This tool proves that any proposition implies itself, meaning for any proposition p, the statement p → p is always true.
conditions: The proposition p can be either true or false.
conclusions: The implication p → p is true.
function_body: theorem imp_self : (a → a) ↔ True := iff_true_intro id

name: imp_false
description: This tool provides a formal proof by contradiction that if a proposition a implies False, then a must be false (¬a).
function_body: theorem imp_false : (a → False) ↔ ¬a := Iff.rfl

name: imp.swap
description: Provides the equivalence of the statements: if a implies b, then b implies a, and vice versa.
conditions: For all a and b, if a is true and b is false
For all a and b, if b is true and a is false
conclusions: b is true and a is false
a is true and b is false
function_body: theorem imp.swap : (a → b → c) ↔ (b → a → c) := ⟨flip, flip⟩

name: imp_not_comm
description: A tool that encapsulates the equivalence between 'If A then not B' and 'If B then not A', demonstrating the contrapositive relationship between the two statements.
conclusions: If A then not B is equivalent to If B then not A
function_body: theorem imp_not_comm : (a → ¬b) ↔ (b → ¬a) := imp.swap

name: imp_congr_left
description: This tool provides a method to transform implications based on the logical equivalence of their antecedents. Given that 'a' and 'b' are logically equivalent, this tool confirms that 'a implies c' is logically equivalent to 'b implies c'.
function_body:
theorem imp_congr_left (h : a ↔ b) : (a → c) ↔ (b → c) :=
  ⟨fun hac ha => hac (h.2 ha), fun hbc ha => hbc (h.1 ha)⟩

name: imp_congr_right
description: A theorem establishing the equivalence of (a → b) and (a → c) given the condition that a implies (b iff c).
function_body:
theorem imp_congr_right (h : a → (b ↔ c)) : (a → b) ↔ (a → c) :=
  ⟨fun hab ha => (h ha).1 (hab ha), fun hcd ha => (h ha).2 (hcd ha)⟩

name: imp_congr_ctx
description: This tool proves that the implication (a → b) is logically equivalent to the implication (c → d) under two conditions: a is logically equivalent to c, and c implies that b is logically equivalent to d.
function_body:
theorem imp_congr_ctx (h₁ : a ↔ c) (h₂ : c → (b ↔ d)) : (a → b) ↔ (c → d) :=
  (imp_congr_left h₁).trans (imp_congr_right h₂)

name: imp_congr
description: This tool provides a theorem for demonstrating that if two pairs of propositions are logically equivalent, then their respective implications are also logically equivalent.
function_body: theorem imp_congr (h₁ : a ↔ c) (h₂ : b ↔ d) : (a → b) ↔ (c → d) := imp_congr_ctx h₁ fun _ => h₂

name: imp_iff_not
description: This tool verifies that the implication 'a implies b' is logically equivalent to the negation of 'a'.
conclusions: a implies b is equivalent to not a
function_body: theorem imp_iff_not (hb : ¬b) : a → b ↔ ¬a := imp_congr_right fun _ => iff_false_intro hb

name: And.symm
description: A theorem that states the conjunction of two propositions is symmetric, meaning the order of the propositions does not affect the truth value of the conjunction.
function_body: theorem And.symm : a ∧ b → b ∧ a | ⟨ha, hb⟩ => ⟨hb, ha⟩

name: And.imp
description: Given functions f and g, and the proof that both preconditions a and b are true, this tool proves that conclusions c and d are both true.
function_body: theorem And.imp (f : a → c) (g : b → d) (h : a ∧ b) : c ∧ d := ⟨f h.1, g h.2⟩

name: And.imp_left
description: A logical tool that deduces `b ∧ c` from `a → b` and `a ∧ c`.
function_body: theorem And.imp_left (h : a → b) : a ∧ c → b ∧ c := fun hc => ⟨h hc.1, hc.2⟩

name: And.imp_right
description: Given three propositions a, b, and c, if a implies b, then c and a together imply c and b.
function_body: theorem And.imp_right (h : a → b) : c ∧ a → c ∧ b := .imp id h

name: and_congr
description: This theorem demonstrates that the conjunction of two pairs of logically equivalent propositions is itself logically equivalent.
function_body:
theorem and_congr (h₁ : a ↔ c) (h₂ : b ↔ d) : a ∧ b ↔ c ∧ d :=
  ⟨And.imp h₁.1 h₂.1, And.imp h₁.2 h₂.2⟩

name: and_comm
description: A tool encapsulating the commutativity of the conjunction operation in logic.
function_body: theorem and_comm : a ∧ b ↔ b ∧ a := And.comm

name: and_congr_right
description: This tool proves the equivalence of an expression involving conjunctions when an implication-equivalence is given.
conditions: a implies b is equivalent to a implies c
conclusions: a and b is equivalent to a and c
function_body: theorem and_congr_right (h : a → (b ↔ c)) : a ∧ b ↔ a ∧ c := ⟨fun ⟨ha, hb⟩ => ⟨ha, (h ha).1 hb⟩, fun ⟨ha, hb⟩ => ⟨ha, (h ha).2 hb⟩⟩

name: and_congr_left
description: A tool that proves if propositions 'a' and 'b' are equivalent when 'c' is true, then 'a' and 'c' are equivalent to 'b' and 'c'.
conditions: If propositions 'a' and 'b' are equivalent when 'c' is true
conclusions: Then 'a' and 'c' are equivalent to 'b' and 'c'
function_body:
theorem and_congr_left (h : c → (a ↔ b)) : a ∧ c ↔ b ∧ c :=
  and_comm.trans <| (and_congr_right h).trans and_comm

name: and_congr_left'
description: A theorem demonstrating how the equivalence of two propositions can be used to show that their conjunctions with a third proposition are also equivalent.
function_body: theorem and_congr_left' (h : a ↔ b) : a ∧ c ↔ b ∧ c := and_congr h .rfl

name: and_congr_right'
description: This tool proves that for given propositions a, b, and c, the conjunction a ∧ b is equivalent to a ∧ c if and only if b is equivalent to c.
function_body: theorem and_congr_right' (h : b ↔ c) : a ∧ b ↔ a ∧ c := and_congr .rfl h

name: and_congr_right_eq
description: A theorem stating that if a ∧ b equals c, then a ∧ b equals a ∧ c.
function_body:
theorem and_congr_right_eq (h : a ∧ b = c) : (a ∧ b) = (a ∧ c) :=
  propext <| and_congr_right fun hc => h hc ▸ .rfl

name: and_congr_left_eq
description: This theorem states that if \( c \) implies \( a \) equals \( b \), then \( a \wedge c \) is logically equivalent to \( b \wedge c \).
function_body:
theorem and_congr_left_eq (h : c → a = b) : (a ∧ c) = (b ∧ c) :=
  propext <| and_congr_left fun hc => h hc ▸ .rfl

name: and_assoc
description: A tool to demonstrate the equivalence of the logical expressions (a ∧ b) ∧ c and a ∧ (b ∧ c).
conclusions: a, b, and c are all true
function_body: theorem and_assoc : (a ∧ b) ∧ c ↔ a ∧ (b ∧ c) := ⟨fun ⟨⟨ha, hb⟩, hc⟩ => ⟨ha, hb, hc⟩, fun ⟨ha, hb, hc⟩ => ⟨⟨ha, hb⟩, hc⟩⟩

name: and_left_comm
description: This tool proves that the conjunction of three logical propositions is commutative when rearranged such that the outermost conjunction is changed.
conclusions: a ∧ (b ∧ c) and b ∧ (a ∧ c) are equivalent
function_body:
theorem and_left_comm : a ∧ (b ∧ c) ↔ b ∧ (a ∧ c) := by
  rw [← and_assoc, ← and_assoc, @and_comm a b]

name: and_right_comm
description: This tool demonstrates the commutative property of conjunction, showing that (a ∧ b) ∧ c is logically equivalent to (a ∧ c) ∧ b.
function_body:
theorem and_right_comm : (a ∧ b) ∧ c ↔ (a ∧ c) ∧ b := by
  simp only [and_left_comm, and_comm]

name: and_rotate
description: This tool proves the equivalence of the logical expression (p ∧ q) ∧ r and q ∧ (r ∧ p) using the associativity and commutativity of conjunction.
function_body:
theorem and_rotate : a ∧ b ∧ c ↔ b ∧ c ∧ a := by
  simp only [and_left_comm, and_comm]

name: and_and_and_comm
description: This tool proves that the logical conjunction of four variables is equivalent whether we group (a ∧ b) with (c ∧ d) or (a ∧ c) with (b ∧ d).
conclusions: (a ∧ b) ∧ c ∧ d ↔ (a ∧ c) ∧ b ∧ d
function_body:
theorem and_and_and_comm : (a ∧ b) ∧ c ∧ d ↔ (a ∧ c) ∧ b ∧ d := by
  rw [← and_assoc, @and_right_comm a, and_assoc]

name: and_and_left
description: This tool proves the associative property of the conjunction operator for three boolean variables a, b, and c. It shows that a ∧ b ∧ c is equivalent to (a ∧ b) ∧ c.
conclusions: a ∧ b ∧ c is equivalent to (a ∧ b) ∧ c
function_body:
theorem and_and_left : a ∧ b ∧ c ↔ (a ∧ b) ∧ a ∧ c := by
  rw [and_and_and_comm, and_self]

name: and_and_right
description: A tool to demonstrate the equivalence between ((a ∧ b) ∧ c) and ((a ∧ c) ∧ b ∧ c) through logical conjunction under the assumption that all involved propositions are true.
function_body:
theorem and_and_right : (a ∧ b) ∧ c ↔ (a ∧ c) ∧ b ∧ c := by
  rw [and_and_and_comm, and_self]

name: and_iff_left_of_imp
description: This tool proves the logical equivalence of (a ∧ b) and a under the condition that a implies b.
conclusions: (a ∧ b) is logically equivalent to a
function_body:
theorem and_iff_left_of_imp (h : a → b) : (a ∧ b) ↔ a :=
  ⟨And.left, fun ha => ⟨ha, h ha⟩⟩

name: and_iff_right_of_imp
description: This tool provides a theorem that shows the logical equivalence of 'a ∧ b' to 'b' given that 'b' implies 'a'.
conclusions: a ∧ b is logically equivalent to b
function_body: theorem and_iff_right_of_imp (h : b → a) : (a ∧ b) ↔ b := ⟨And.right, fun hb => ⟨h hb, hb⟩⟩

name: and_iff_left
description: This tool proves that for any two logical propositions a and b, if both a and b are true, then a is true.
function_body: theorem and_iff_left (hb : b) : a ∧ b ↔ a := and_iff_left_of_imp fun _ => hb

name: and_iff_right
description: This tool provides a theorem that states for any proposition a, a ∧ b is equivalent to b.
conclusions: a ∧ b is equivalent to b.
function_body: theorem and_iff_right (ha : a) : a ∧ b ↔ b := and_iff_right_of_imp fun _ => ha

name: and_iff_left_iff_imp
description: This tool provides a theorem that states the equivalence between a conjunction's implication to one of its components and a direct implication between the components.
function_body:
theorem and_iff_left_iff_imp : ((a ∧ b) ↔ a) ↔ (a → b) :=
  ⟨fun h ha => (h.2 ha).2, and_iff_left_of_imp⟩

name: and_iff_right_iff_imp
description: This theorem tool allows you to deduce that (a ∧ b) ↔ b is true if and only if b → a is true.
function_body:
theorem and_iff_right_iff_imp : ((a ∧ b) ↔ b) ↔ (b → a) :=
  ⟨fun h ha => (h.2 ha).1, and_iff_right_of_imp⟩

name: iff_self_and
description: A tool to prove the equivalence between the statements 'p if and only if p and q' and 'If p, then q'.
conditions: p if and only if p and q
conclusions: The statements 'p if and only if p and q' and 'If p, then q' are equivalent.
function_body:
theorem iff_self_and : (p ↔ p ∧ q) ↔ (p → q) := by 
  rw [@Iff.comm p, and_iff_left_iff_imp]

name: iff_and_self
description: This tool demonstrates the logical equivalence between (p ↔ q ∧ p) and (p → q) using logical equivalence and rewriting rules.
conditions: There are two propositions, p and q.
conclusions: The equivalence (p ↔ q ∧ p) is equivalent to (p → q).
function_body: theorem iff_and_self : (p ↔ q ∧ p) ↔ (p → q) := by rw [and_comm, iff_self_and]

name: and_congr_right_iff
description: This tool verifies the logical equivalence between (a ∧ b) ↔ (a ∧ c) and a → (b ↔ c).
function_body:
theorem and_congr_right_iff : (a ∧ b ↔ a ∧ c) ↔ (a → (b ↔ c)) :=
  ⟨fun h ha => by simp [ha] at h; exact h, and_congr_right⟩

name: and_congr_left_iff
description: A tool for proving equivalence of conjunctions under the assumption of the equivalence of their constituents and a condition.
function_body:
theorem and_congr_left_iff : (a ∧ c ↔ b ∧ c) ↔ c → (a ↔ b) := by
  simp only [and_comm, ← and_congr_right_iff]

name: and_self_left
description: This tool simplifies a conjunction where a term is repeated on the left side of another conjunction, effectively removing the redundant repetition.
conditions: The conjunction operation must be associative.
The conjunction operation must be idempotent.
conclusions: The expression a ∧ a ∧ b is equivalent to a ∧ b.
function_body:
theorem and_self_left : a ∧ a ∧ b ↔ a ∧ b :=
  ⟨fun h => ⟨h.1, h.2.2⟩, fun h => ⟨h.1, h.1, h.2⟩⟩

name: and_self_right
description: This theorem states that the conjunction of (a and b) and b is logically equivalent to a and b. It leverages the associative and idempotent properties of conjunction.
conditions: Two arbitrary propositions a and b
conclusions: (a ∧ b) ∧ b is logically equivalent to a ∧ b
function_body:
theorem and_self_right : (a ∧ b) ∧ b ↔ a ∧ b :=
  ⟨fun h => ⟨h.1.1, h.2⟩, fun h => ⟨⟨h.1, h.2⟩, h.2⟩⟩

name: not_and_of_not_left
description: A theorem stating that if the first proposition is false, then the conjunction of the first and second propositions must also be false.
conclusions: The conjunction of the first and second propositions (a ∧ b) is false
function_body: theorem not_and_of_not_left (b : Prop) : ¬a → ¬(a ∧ b) := mt And.left

name: not_and_of_not_right
description: A tool to demonstrate that if proposition 'a' is false, then the conjunction 'a ∧ b' is also false for any proposition 'b'.
function_body: theorem not_and_of_not_right (a : Prop) {b : Prop} : ¬a → ¬(a ∧ b) := mt And.left

name: and_not_self
description: This tool verifies that a proposition and its negation cannot both be true simultaneously.
function_body: theorem and_not_self : ¬(a ∧ ¬a) | ⟨ha, hn⟩ => hn ha

name: not_and_self
description: This tool shows the impossibility of both a statement and its negation being true simultaneously.
function_body: theorem not_and_self : ¬(¬a ∧ a) | ⟨hn, ha⟩ => hn ha

name: and_not_self_iff
description: This tool proves that the conjunction of a proposition and its negation is always false.
function_body: theorem and_not_self_iff (a : Prop) : a ∧ ¬a ↔ False := iff_false_intro and_not_self

name: not_and_self_iff
description: A tool that proves that a proposition and its negation being true is logically equivalent to False.
function_body: theorem not_and_self_iff (a : Prop) : ¬a ∧ a ↔ False := iff_false_intro (λ ⟨h₁, h₂⟩, h₁ h₂)

name: not_not_em
description: A tool to demonstrate that the statement 'It is not the case that either a proposition is true or its negation is true' is false.
conditions: Assume the statement 'It is not the case that either a proposition is true or its negation is true' is true.
Every proposition is either true or false.
conclusions: The statement 'It is not the case that either a proposition is true or its negation is true' is false
function_body: theorem not_not_em (a : Prop) : ¬¬(a ∨ ¬a) := fun h => h (.inr (h ∘ .inl))

name: Or.symm
description: This tool demonstrates the commutative property of logical OR, showing that a ∨ b is equivalent to b ∨ a.
function_body: theorem Or.symm : a ∨ b → b ∨ a := .rec .inr .inl

name: Or.imp
description: A tool to prove that the disjunction of images under functions f and g of a union element h will yield the union of their codomains.
function_body: theorem Or.imp (f : a → c) (g : b → d) (h : a ∨ b) : c ∨ d := h.elim (inl ∘ f) (inr ∘ g)

name: Or.imp_left
description: This tool demonstrates that the logical implication (a ∨ c) → (b ∨ c) is a tautology. It shows that if either statement a or c is true, then it necessarily implies that either statement b or c is true.
function_body: theorem Or.imp_left (f : a → b) : a ∨ c → b ∨ c := .imp f id

name: Or.imp_right
description: This theorem proves that the implication (a ∨ b) → (a ∨ c) holds true for any boolean variables a, b, and c using the truth table method, showing it's a tautology.
conditions: a, b, and c are boolean variables
function_body: theorem Or.imp_right (f : b → c) : a ∨ b → a ∨ c := .imp id f

name: or_congr
description: This tool proves that if two pairs of propositions are logically equivalent, then the disjunctions of these pairs are also logically equivalent.
function_body: theorem or_congr (h₁ : a ↔ c) (h₂ : b ↔ d) : (a ∨ b) ↔ (c ∨ d) := ⟨.imp h₁.1 h₂.1, .imp h₁.2 h₂.2⟩

name: or_congr_left
description: A theorem stating that if two propositions a and b are equivalent, then the disjunction of a or c is equivalent to the disjunction of b or c.
conclusions: a or c is equivalent to b or c
function_body: theorem or_congr_left (h : a ↔ b) : a ∨ c ↔ b ∨ c := or_congr h rfl

name: exists_congr_left
description: This theorem states that if two elements a and b are equal, then the existence of an x for which a equals x is equivalent to the existence of an x for which b equals x.
conclusions: ∃ x, a = x ↔ ∃ x, b = x
function_body:
theorem exists_congr_left (h : a = b) : ∃ x, a = x ↔ ∃ x, b = x := by
  simp [h]
  apply exists.congr .rfl

name: Or.comm
description: This tool demonstrates the commutative property of the logical 'or' operation, showing that the order of operands does not affect the result.
function_body: theorem Or.comm : a ∨ b ↔ b ∨ a := ⟨Or.symm, Or.symm⟩

name: or_comm
description: This tool proves the commutative property of the logical disjunction, showing that a ∨ b is equivalent to b ∨ a.
function_body: theorem or_comm : a ∨ b ↔ b ∨ a := Or.comm

name: or_assoc
description: This tool verifies the associativity property of disjunction in propositional logic, i.e., the equivalence of (a ∨ b) ∨ c and a ∨ (b ∨ c).
function_body:
theorem or_assoc : (a ∨ b) ∨ c ↔ a ∨ (b ∨ c) :=
  ⟨.rec (.imp_right .inl) (.inr ∘ .inr), .rec (.inl ∘ .inl) (.imp_left .inr)⟩

name: Or.resolve_left
description: A tool that concludes B is true when given A or B is true and A is false.
function_body: theorem Or.resolve_left {a b : Prop} (h: a ∨ b) (na : ¬a) : b := h.elim (absurd · na) id

name: Or.neg_resolve_left
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem that given a disjunction of the form not(a) or b, if a is true, then b must also be true.
function_body: theorem Or.neg_resolve_left (h : ¬a ∨ b) (ha : a) : b := h.elim (absurd ha) id

name: Or.resolve_right
description: A logical tool that deduces the truth of proposition 'a' given that 'a or b' is true and 'b' is false.
function_body: theorem Or.resolve_right {a b : Prop} (h: a ∨ b) (nb : ¬b) : a := h.elim id (absurd · nb)

name: Or.neg_resolve_right
description: Solves for 'a' given conditions 'a ∨ ¬b' and 'b'. The resolution uses the fact that if 'b' is true, then '¬b' must be false, thereby leaving 'a' to be true.
function_body: theorem Or.neg_resolve_right (h : a ∨ ¬b) (nb : b) : a := h.elim id (absurd nb)

name: or_left_comm
description: This tool shows the equivalence between the left and right associativity of the logical or operator.
conditions: logical or operator is associative and commutative
function_body: theorem or_left_comm : a ∨ (b ∨ c) ↔ b ∨ (a ∨ c) := by rw [← or_assoc, ← or_assoc, @or_comm a b]

name: or_right_comm
description: This tool verifies the logical equivalence of (a ∨ b) ∨ c and (a ∨ c) ∨ b using the commutativity and associativity of logical disjunction.
conditions: a, b, and c are arbitrary propositions
conclusions: (a ∨ b) ∨ c is logically equivalent to (a ∨ c) ∨ b
function_body: theorem or_right_comm : (a ∨ b) ∨ c ↔ (a ∨ c) ∨ b := by rw [or_assoc, or_assoc, @or_comm b]

name: or_or_or_comm
description: A tool that proves the equivalence of $(a \lor b) \lor c \lor d$ and $(a \lor c) \lor b \lor d$ using associativity and commutativity of logical or (\lor).
conclusions: (a ∨ b) ∨ c ∨ d ↔ (a ∨ c) ∨ b ∨ d
function_body:
theorem or_or_or_comm : (a ∨ b) ∨ c ∨ d ↔ (a ∨ c) ∨ b ∨ d := by
  rw [← or_assoc, @or_right_comm a, or_assoc]

name: or_or_distrib_left
description: This tool demonstrates the equivalence of the disjunction a ∨ b ∨ c and (a ∨ b) ∨ a ∨ c by utilizing the commutativity and idempotency properties of disjunction.
conclusions: a ∨ b ∨ c ↔ (a ∨ b) ∨ a ∨ c
function_body: theorem or_or_distrib_left : a ∨ b ∨ c ↔ (a ∨ b) ∨ a ∨ c := by rw [or_or_or_comm, or_self]

name: or_or_distrib_right
description: This theorem shows the logical equivalence between (a ∨ b) ∨ c and (a ∨ c) ∨ b ∨ c by using the equivalence of both expressions to a ∨ b ∨ c.
conclusions: (a ∨ b) ∨ c is logically equivalent to (a ∨ c) ∨ b ∨ c
function_body: theorem or_or_distrib_right : (a ∨ b) ∨ c ↔ (a ∨ c) ∨ b ∨ c := by rw [or_or_or_comm, or_self]

name: or_rotate
description: A tool that demonstrates the rotation of operands in a disjunction is equivalent.
function_body: theorem or_rotate : a ∨ b ∨ c ↔ b ∨ c ∨ a := by simp only [or_left_comm, Or.comm]

name: or_iff_right_of_imp
description: This tool verifies the logical equivalence that for any propositions a and b, the disjunction 'a or b' is equivalent to b, given that a implies b.
conclusions: a ∨ b is logically equivalent to b
function_body: theorem or_iff_right_of_imp (ha : a → b) : (a ∨ b) ↔ b := ⟨Or.rec ha id, .inr⟩

name: or_iff_left_of_imp
description: This tool proves that if proposition b implies proposition a, then a or b is logically equivalent to a.
conclusions: a or b is equivalent to a
function_body: theorem or_iff_left_of_imp (hb : b → a) : (a ∨ b) ↔ a := ⟨Or.rec id hb, .inl⟩

name: not_or_intro
description: This tool proves that if neither of two propositions is true, then their disjunction is also false.
function_body: theorem not_or_intro {a b : Prop} (ha : ¬a) (hb : ¬b) : ¬(a ∨ b) := (·.elim ha hb)

name: or_iff_left_iff_imp
description: This tool provides an equivalence between the logical statements (a ∨ b ↔ a) and (b → a). It shows that given (a ∨ b ↔ a), we can infer (b → a) and vice versa.
conditions: a ∨ b ↔ a or b → a
function_body:
theorem or_iff_left_iff_imp : (a ∨ b ↔ a) ↔ (b → a) :=
  ⟨fun h hb => h.1 (Or.inr hb), or_iff_left_of_imp⟩

name: or_iff_right_iff_imp
description: A tool to prove the equivalence of 'a ∨ b ↔ b' and 'a → b', using logical equivalences and transformations.
function_body:
theorem or_iff_right_iff_imp : (a ∨ b ↔ b) ↔ (a → b) := by
  rw [or_comm, or_iff_left_iff_imp]

name: or_iff_left
description: This tool verifies the logical equivalence between (a ∨ b) and a under the condition that b is false.
function_body: theorem or_iff_left (hb : ¬b) : a ∨ b ↔ a := or_iff_left_iff_imp.2 hb.elim

name: or_iff_right
description: This tool proves that 'a ∨ b' is equivalent to 'b' if 'a' is false.
conclusions: a ∨ b is equivalent to b
function_body: theorem or_iff_right (ha : ¬a) : a ∨ b ↔ b := or_iff_right_iff_imp.2 ha.elim

name: not_imp_of_and_not
description: A tool to assert that (p and not q) implies not (if p then q).
conclusions: if p then q is false
function_body:
theorem not_imp_of_and_not : a ∧ ¬b → ¬(a → b)
  | ⟨ha, hb⟩, h => hb <| h ha

name: imp_and
description: This tool provides the equivalence between the conjunction of two propositions and the conjunction of their implications.
function_body:
theorem imp_and {α} : (α → b ∧ c) ↔ (α → b) ∧ (α → c) :=
  ⟨fun h => ⟨fun ha => (h ha).1, fun ha => (h ha).2⟩, fun h ha => ⟨h.1 ha, h.2 ha⟩⟩

name: and_imp
description: This tool demonstrates the logical equivalence between the formulas (a ∧ b) → c and (a → b) → c by proving the equivalence in both directions.
conclusions: (a ∧ b) → c is logically equivalent to (a → b) → c
function_body:
theorem and_imp : (a ∧ b → c) ↔ (a → b → c) :=
  ⟨fun h ha hb => h ⟨ha, hb⟩, fun h ⟨ha, hb⟩ => h ha hb⟩

name: not_and
description: A tool that demonstrates the logical equivalence between the negation of the conjunction of two propositions and the implication of one proposition with the negation of the other.
function_body: theorem not_and : ¬(a ∧ b) ↔ (a → ¬b) := and_imp

name: not_and'
description: This tool encapsulates the logical equivalence between ¬(a ∧ b) and (b → ¬a). It shows that the negation of the conjunction of a and b is logically equivalent to b implying the negation of a.
function_body: theorem not_and' : ¬(a ∧ b) ↔ b → ¬a := not_and.trans imp_not_comm

name: and_or_left
description: This tool proves that the conjunction of a term and a disjunction is logically equivalent to the disjunction of the conjunctions of the term with each part of the disjunction.
function_body:
theorem and_or_left : a ∧ (b ∨ c) ↔ (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c) :=
  ⟨fun ⟨ha, hbc⟩ => hbc.imp (.intro ha) (.intro ha), Or.rec (.imp_right .inl) (.imp_right .inr)⟩

name: or_and_right
description: A theorem that shows the equivalence between (a ∨ b) ∧ c and (a ∧ c) ∨ (b ∧ c) using the distributive law.
function_body:
theorem or_and_right : (a ∨ b) ∧ c ↔ (a ∧ c) ∨ (b ∧ c) := by
  simp [and_comm, and_or_left]

name: or_and_left
description: This tool proves that the disjunction of a proposition with the conjunction of two other propositions is logically equivalent to the conjunction of the disjunctions of the first proposition with each of the others.
conditions: Propositions a, b, and c in a logical system
conclusions: \(a \lor (b \land c) \) is logically equivalent to \((a \lor b) \land (a \lor c) \)
function_body:
theorem or_and_left : a ∨ (b ∧ c) ↔ (a ∨ b) ∧ (a ∨ c) :=
  ⟨Or.rec (fun ha => ⟨.inl ha, .inl ha⟩) (.imp .inr .inr),
   And.rec <| .rec (fun _ => .inl ·) (.imp_right ∘ .intro)⟩

name: and_or_right
description: This tool provides a proof of the logical equivalence between (a ∧ b) ∨ c and (a ∨ c) ∧ (b ∨ c), based on associativity and commutativity properties of ∨ and ∧.
conditions: Logical expressions involving conjunctions (∧) and disjunctions (∨)
conclusions: Expression (a ∧ b) ∨ c is logically equivalent to (a ∨ c) ∧ (b ∨ c)
function_body:
theorem and_or_right : (a ∧ b) ∨ c ↔ (a ∨ c) ∧ (b ∨ c) := by
  simp [or_comm, or_and_left]

name: or_imp
description: A tool that demonstrates the logical equivalence between (a ∨ b → c) and (a → c) ∧ (b → c). It shows that for any propositions a, b, and c, if the disjunction implies c, then both individual propositions imply c, and vice versa.
conditions: a, b, and c are propositions
function_body:
theorem or_imp : (a ∨ b → c) ↔ (a → c) ∧ (b → c) :=
  ⟨fun h => ⟨h ∘ .inl, h ∘ .inr⟩, fun ⟨ha, hb⟩ => Or.rec ha hb⟩

name: not_or
description: This tool verifies that the negation of a disjunction (p or q) is logically equivalent to the conjunction of the negations (not p and not q).
function_body: theorem not_or : ¬(p ∨ q) ↔ ¬p ∧ ¬q := or_imp

name: not_and_of_not_or_not
description: This tool proves that if the disjunction of two statements is false, then the conjunction of those statements is also false.
function_body: theorem not_and_of_not_or_not (h : ¬(a ∨ b)) : ¬(a ∧ b) := fun hab => h (Or.inl hab.1)

name: or_self_left
description: Simplifies the logical expression by removing redundant disjunctions, proving that a ∨ a ∨ b is equivalent to a ∨ b.
conditions: a ∨ a ∨ b is true or a ∨ b is true
conclusions: a ∨ a ∨ b is logically equivalent to a ∨ b
function_body: theorem or_self_left : a ∨ a ∨ b ↔ a ∨ b := ⟨.rec .inl id, .rec .inl (.inr ∘ .inr)⟩

name: or_self_right
description: A theorem stating that the logical OR of (a or b) with b is logically equivalent to a or b.
conclusions: (a ∨ b) ∨ b is equivalent to a ∨ b
function_body: theorem or_self_right : (a ∨ b) ∨ b ↔ a ∨ b := ⟨.rec id .inr, .rec (.inl ∘ .inl) .inr⟩

name: forall_imp
description: This tool proves that if for all elements a, p(a) implies q(a), and p(a) holds for all a, then q(a) must also hold for all a.
conditions: For all a, if p(a) is true, then q(a) is also true.
For all a, p(a) is true.
conclusions: For all a, q(a) is true.
function_body:
theorem forall_imp (h : ∀ a, p a → q a) : (∀ a, p a) → ∀ a, q a :=
fun h' a => h a (h' a)

name: forall_exists_index
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem which states that ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) is logically equivalent to (∀x P(x)) → (∀x Q(x)). This can be utilized to transform and reason about universally quantified implications.
conditions: Two propositions P(x) and Q(x) are given
Universal quantification is applied over a variable x
conclusions: The equivalence ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) ↔ (∀x P(x)) → (∀x Q(x)) holds
function_body:
theorem forall_exists_index {q : (∃ x, p x) → Prop} :
    (∀ h, q h) ↔ ∀ x (h : p x), q ⟨x, h⟩ :=
  ⟨fun h x hpx => h ⟨x, hpx⟩, fun h ⟨x, hpx⟩ => h x hpx⟩

name: Exists.imp
description: This tool proves that if for all elements, property p implies property q, then the existence of an element with property p implies the existence of an element with property q.
conditions: For all a, p(a) implies q(a)
There exists an a such that p(a) holds
conclusions: There exists an a such that q(a) holds
function_body:
theorem Exists.imp (h : ∀ a, p a → q a) : (∃ a, p a) → ∃ a, q a
  | ⟨a, hp⟩ => ⟨a, h a hp⟩

name: Exists.imp'
description: This tool proves that if there exists an element a in a set such that p(a) holds, then there exists an element b in the set such that q(b) holds, given a function f and the implication p(a) ⇒ q(f(a)).
conditions: There exists an element a such that p(a) holds.
For all a, p(a) implies q(f(a)).
conclusions: There exists an element b such that q(b) holds.
function_body:
theorem Exists.imp' {β} {q : β → Prop} (f : α → β) (hpq : ∀ a, p a → q (f a)) : (∃ a, p a) → ∃ b, q b
  | ⟨_, hp⟩ => ⟨_, hpq _ hp⟩

name: exists_imp
description: This tool encapsulates the logical equivalence between an implication involving an existential quantifier and a universal quantifier. Specifically, it demonstrates that if the implication that there exists an x such that P(x) implies Q(x) is true, then it is equivalent to stating that for all x, P(x) implies Q(x).
conditions: There exists an x such that P(x)
The implication (∃ x, P(x)) → Q(x) holds
function_body: theorem exists_imp : ((∃ x, p x) → b) ↔ ∀ x, p x → b := forall_exists_index

name: exists_const
description: A theorem that establishes the equivalence between the existence of an element in a nonempty type satisfying a property and the property itself.
function_body:
theorem exists_const (α) [i : Nonempty α] : (∃ _ : α, b) ↔ b :=
  ⟨fun ⟨_, h⟩ => h, i.elim Exists.intro⟩

name: forall_congr'
description: A logical tool that states the equivalence between the universal quantifications of predicates p and q over a domain, given that p(x) and q(x) are logically equivalent for all x.
function_body:
theorem forall_congr' (h : ∀ a, p a ↔ q a) : (∀ a, p a) ↔ ∀ a, q a :=
  ⟨fun H a => (h a).1 (H a), fun H a => (h a).2 (H a)⟩

name: exists_congr
description: This tool takes in predicates P(x) and Q(x), and if P(x) is equivalent to Q(x) for all x, it concludes that the existence of an x such that P(x) is true is equivalent to the existence of an x such that Q(x) is true.
conditions: For all x, P(x) is equivalent to Q(x)
conclusions: The existence of an x such that P(x) is true is equivalent to the existence of an x such that Q(x) is true
function_body:
theorem exists_congr (h : ∀ a, p a ↔ q a) : (∃ a, p a) ↔ ∃ a, q a :=
  ⟨Exists.imp fun x => (h x).1, Exists.imp fun x => (h x).2⟩

name: forall₂_congr
description: This tool provides a theorem that establishes a logical equivalence between two universally quantified predicates on some type, provided that the predicates are equivalent for all instances of the type.
conditions: p(a, b) is a predicate on some type
q(a, b) is a predicate on some type
p(a, b) is equivalent to q(a, b) for all a and b
conclusions: p(a, b) for all a and b if and only if q(a, b) for all a and b
function_body:
theorem forall₂_congr {p q : ∀ a, β a → Prop} (h : ∀ a b, p a b ↔ q a b) :
    (∀ a b, p a b) ↔ ∀ a b, q a b :=
  forall_congr' fun a => forall_congr' <| h a

name: exists₂_congr
description: This tool states that if two properties p and q are equivalent for any element a and any proof b, then the existence of an element with property p is equivalent to the existence of an element with property q.
conditions: ∀ a b, p(a, b) ↔ q(a, b)
conclusions: (∃ a b, p(a, b)) ↔ (∃ a b, q(a, b))
function_body:
theorem exists₂_congr {p q : ∀ a, β a → Prop} (h : ∀ a b, p a b ↔ q a b) :
  (∃ a b, p a b) ↔ ∃ a b, q a b :=
  exists_congr fun a => exists_congr <| h a

name: forall₃_congr
description: This tool proves that if two logical predicates are equivalent for all arguments, then the universally quantified statements of those predicates are also equivalent.
conditions: ∀ a, b, c, p(a, b, c) ↔ q(a, b, c)
conclusions: ∀ a, b, c, p(a, b, c) ↔ ∀ a, b, c, q(a, b, c)
function_body: theorem forall₃_congr {p q : ∀ a b, γ a b → Prop} (h : ∀ a b c, p a b c ↔ q a b c) : (∀ a b c, p a b c) ↔ ∀ a b c, q a b c := forall_congr' fun a => forall₂_congr <| h a

name: exists₃_congr
description: This tool asserts that if two ternary predicates are equivalent, then the existence of a witness for one predicate implies the existence of a witness for the other predicate.
conditions: Two ternary predicates p and q
Equivalence between predicates p and q
conclusions: The existence of a witness for one predicate implies the existence of a witness for the other predicate
function_body: theorem exists₃_congr {p q : ∀ a b, γ a b → Prop} (h : ∀ a b c, p a b c ↔ q a b c) : (∃ a b c, p a b c) ↔ ∃ a b c, q a b c := exists_congr fun a => exists₂_congr <| h a

name: forall₄_congr
description: A theorem stating that if two predicates on four arguments are equivalent for all values of their arguments, then for any four arguments, one predicate holds if and only if the other predicate holds.
conditions: p and q are predicates on four arguments
p and q are equivalent for all values of their arguments
conclusions: For any four arguments, p holds if and only if q holds
function_body: theorem forall₄_congr {p q : ∀ a b c d, Prop} (h : ∀ a b c d, p a b c d ↔ q a b c d) : (∀ a b c d, p a b c d) ↔ (∀ a b c d, q a b c d) := forall_congr' (fun a => forall₃_congr (h a))

name: exists₄_congr
description: A theorem that states if two predicates with four arguments are logically equivalent for all arguments, then the existence of one predicate implies the existence of the other.
conditions: For all a, b, c, d, p(a, b, c, d) is equivalent to q(a, b, c, d)
conclusions: Existence of a, b, c, d such that p(a, b, c, d) is equivalent to the existence of a, b, c, d such that q(a, b, c, d)
function_body:
theorem exists₄_congr {p q : ∀ a b c, δ a b c → Prop} (h : ∀ a b c d, p a b c d ↔ q a b c d) :
    (∃ a b c d, p a b c d) ↔ ∃ a b c d, q a b c d :=
  exists_congr fun a => exists₃_congr <| h a

name: forall₅_congr
description: This tool asserts the equivalence of two statements involving universal quantifiers over five variables and a proposition that depends on these variables.
conditions: For all `a`, `b`, `c`, `d`, and `e`, if `p a b c d e` holds, then `q a b c d e` holds.
For all `a`, `b`, `c`, `d`, and `e`, if `q a b c d e` holds, then `p a b c d e` holds.
conclusions: The statements involving universal quantifiers over five variables are equivalent: ∀ a b c d e, `p a b c d e` holds if and only if ∀ a b c d e, `q a b c d e` holds.
function_body: theorem forall₅_congr {p q : ∀ a b c d e, Prop} (h : ∀ a b c d e, p a b c d e ↔ q a b c d e) : (∀ a b c d e, p a b c d e) ↔ ∀ a b c d e, q a b c d e := forall_congr' fun a => forall₄_congr <| h a

name: exists₅_congr
description: A theorem that states if two predicates on five variables are equivalent for all values of the variables, then the existence of a tuple satisfying one predicate is equivalent to the existence of a tuple satisfying the other predicate.
conditions: For any values of the five variables a, b, c, d, and e, the predicates p and q are equivalent: p(a, b, c, d, e) ⇔ q(a, b, c, d, e).
conclusions: The existence of a set of values a, b, c, d, and e that satisfy p(a, b, c, d, e) is equivalent to the existence of a set of values a, b, c, d, and e that satisfy q(a, b, c, d, e).
function_body: theorem exists₅_congr {p q : ∀ a b c d e, Prop} (h : ∀ a b c d e, p a b c d e ↔ q a b c d e) : (∃ a b c d e, p a b c d e) ↔ ∃ a b c d e, q a b c d e := exists_congr (λ a, exists_congr (λ b, exists_congr (λ c, exists_congr (λ d, exists_congr (λ e, h a b c d e)))))

name: not_exists
description: A tool that verifies the equivalence between the negation of the existence of an element satisfying a predicate and the universal negation of the predicate for all elements.
conditions: The negation of the statement 'there exists x such that p(x) is true'.
conclusions: The statement 'for all x, p(x) is false'.
function_body: theorem not_exists : (¬∃ x, p x) ↔ ∀ x, ¬p x := exists_imp

name: forall_not_of_not_exists
description: A tool that proves if it is not the case that there exists some x such that P(x) is true, then for all x, P(x) is false.
conditions: It is not the case that there exists some x such that P(x) is true
conclusions: For all x, P(x) is false
function_body: theorem forall_not_of_not_exists (hne : ¬∃ x, p x) (x) : ¬p x | hp => hne ⟨x, hp⟩

name: forall_and
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem that states that the universal quantifier of a conjunction (∀ x, p x ∧ q x) is logically equivalent to the conjunction of universal quantifiers (∀ x, p x) ∧ (∀ x, q x).
conditions: p x ∧ q x for each x in the domain
conclusions: (∀ x, p x ∧ q x) ↔ (∀ x, p x) ∧ (∀ x, q x)
function_body:
theorem forall_and : (∀ x, p x ∧ q x) ↔ (∀ x, p x) ∧ (∀ x, q x) :=
  ⟨fun h => ⟨fun x => (h x).1, fun x => (h x).2⟩, fun ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ x => ⟨h₁ x, h₂ x⟩⟩

name: exists_or
description: This tool encapsulates a theorem in predicate logic which states that there exists an x such that either p(x) or q(x) is true if and only if either there exists an x such that p(x) is true, or there exists an x such that q(x) is true.
conditions: (∃ x, p x) ∨ ∃ x, q x
conclusions: (∃ x, p x) ∨ ∃ x, q x
function_body:
theorem exists_or : (∃ x, p x ∨ q x) ↔ (∃ x, p x) ∨ ∃ x, q x :=
  ⟨fun | ⟨x, .inl h⟩ => .inl ⟨x, h⟩ | ⟨x, .inr h⟩ => .inr ⟨x, h⟩,
   fun | .inl ⟨x, h⟩ => ⟨x, .inl h⟩ | .inr ⟨x, h⟩ => ⟨x, .inr h⟩⟩

name: exists_false
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem that there does not exist an element of any type α that satisfies the property False.
conditions: Assume there is an element 'a' of type α that satisfies the property False.
conclusions: It is impossible for any element of type α to satisfy the property False.
function_body: theorem exists_false : ¬(∃ _a : α, False) := fun ⟨_, h⟩ => h

name: forall_const
description: This tool demonstrates that under the condition of a nonempty type α, a function from α to any type b is equivalent to the type b itself.
conclusions: A function from α to b is equivalent to b
function_body:
theorem forall_const (α : Sort _) [i : Nonempty α] : (α → b) ↔ b :=
  ⟨i.elim, fun hb _ => hb⟩

name: Exists.nonempty
description: This theorem asserts that if there exists an element x in the domain α such that the proposition p(x) holds true, then the set of all such x is nonempty.
conditions: There exists an element x in the domain α such that the proposition p(x) is true.
conclusions: The set of all x such that p(x) is true is nonempty.
function_body: theorem Exists.nonempty : (∃ x, p x) → Nonempty α | ⟨x, _⟩ => ⟨x⟩

name: Exists.choose_spec
description: A theorem that asserts if there exists an element satisfying a given property, then the element chosen by the classical 'some' function satisfies the same property.
conditions: There exists an element x such that the property p(x) holds.
conclusions: The element chosen by classical.some satisfies the property p(x).
function_body: theorem Exists.choose_spec {p : α → Prop} (P : ∃ a, p a) : p P.choose := Classical.choose_spec P

name: not_forall_of_exists_not
description: A tool that leverages the logical equivalence between the negation of a universal quantification and the existential quantification of the negation of a property within a given set.
conditions: A property p is defined over a set α.
The negation of the universal quantification of p over set α holds.
conclusions: The existential quantification of the negation of p over set α holds.
function_body:
theorem not_forall_of_exists_not {p : α → Prop} : (∃ x, ¬p x) → ¬∀ x, p x
  | ⟨x, hn⟩, h => hn (h x)

name: forall_eq
description: A theorem that states for any predicate p(x) and element a', (∀ x. x = a' → p(x)) is equivalent to p(a').
function_body:
theorem forall_eq {p : α → Prop} {a' : α} : (∀ a, a = a' → p a) ↔ p a' :=
  ⟨fun h => h a' rfl, fun h _ e => e.symm ▸ h⟩

name: forall_eq'
description: A tool that provides a proof for the equivalence between universal conditional statements involving equality and a direct statement.
conditions: a' is an element of type α
p is a property or predicate on α
conclusions: The statements (∀ a, a' = a → p a) and p a' are equivalent
function_body: theorem forall_eq' {a' : α} : (∀ a, a' = a → p a) ↔ p a' := by simp [@eq_comm _ a']

name: exists_eq
description: A theorem that asserts the existence of an element 'a' such that 'a' equals 'a'.
conclusions: There exists an 'a' such that 'a = a'
function_body: theorem exists_eq : ∃ a, a = a := ⟨_, rfl⟩

name: exists_eq'
description: This tool proves the existence of an element 'a' such that a' equals a, using basic properties of equality.
conditions: Element 'a' and its prime, 'a'', are defined within the context
conclusions: There exists an element a such that a' = a
function_body: theorem exists_eq' : ∃ a, a' = a := ⟨_, rfl⟩

name: exists_eq_left
description: A theorem that investigates the existence of a real number x such that x^2 = 2 and x < 0, and demonstrates the logical implications of the conditions.
function_body: theorem exists_eq_left : (∃ a, a = a' ∧ p a) ↔ p a' := ⟨fun ⟨_, e, h⟩ => e ▸ h, fun h => ⟨_, rfl, h⟩⟩

name: exists_eq_right
description: This tool establishes the equivalence between the existence of an element 'x' that satisfies both the predicate 'p(x)' and 'x = a', and the satisfaction of the predicate 'p(a)'.
conditions: A propositional function p(x) is defined
conclusions: The statement (∃ x, p(x) ∧ x=a) ↔ p(a) holds true
function_body:
theorem exists_eq_right : (∃ a, p a ∧ a = a') ↔ p a' :=
  (exists_congr <| by exact fun a => And.comm).trans exists_eq_left

name: exists_and_left
description: This tool establishes the logical equivalence between the existence of an element satisfying both predicates P and Q, and the conjunction of P being true with the existence of an element satisfying Q.
conditions: There exists an element x such that P(x) and Q(x) are both true.
P(x) is true and there exists an element x such that Q(x) is true.
conclusions: There exists an element x such that P(x) and Q(x) are both true.
P(x) is true and there exists an element x such that Q(x) is true.
function_body: theorem exists_and_left : (∃ x, b ∧ p x) ↔ b ∧ (∃ x, p x) := ⟨fun ⟨x, h, hp⟩ => ⟨h, x, hp⟩, fun ⟨h, x, hp⟩ => ⟨x, h, hp⟩⟩

name: exists_and_right
description: This tool proves the equivalence between the existence of an element satisfying a predicate and a proposition, and the conjunction of the proposition with the existence of an element satisfying the predicate.
conclusions: (∃ x, p x ∧ b) is equivalent to (∃ x, p x) ∧ b.
function_body: theorem exists_and_right : (∃ x, p x ∧ b) ↔ (∃ x, p x) ∧ b := by simp [And.comm]

name: exists_eq_left'
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem that establishes the equivalence between the existence of an element a such that a' equals a and the satisfaction of a predicate p by a', and the direct satisfaction of the predicate p by a'.
function_body: theorem exists_eq_left' : (∃ a, a' = a ∧ p a) ↔ p a' := by simp [@eq_comm _ a']

name: forall_eq_or_imp
description: A tool to prove the equivalence between a condition involving a universal quantifier over a disjunction implying a predicate and the conjunction of a specific instance of the predicate with a universal implication involving another predicate.
conditions: a, a' are variables of type A
p and q are predicates on A
function_body:
theorem forall_eq_or_imp : (∀ a, a = a' ∨ q a → p a) ↔ p a' ∧ ∀ a, q a → p a := by
  simp only [or_imp, forall_and, forall_eq]

name: exists_eq_or_imp
description: This tool encapsulates a logical equivalence theorem regarding the existence and conjunction statements involving logical OR and equality.
function_body:
theorem exists_eq_or_imp : (∃ a, (a = a' ∨ q a) ∧ p a) ↔ p a' ∨ ∃ a, q a ∧ p a := by
  simp only [or_and_right, exists_or, exists_eq_left]

name: exists_eq_right_right
description: This tool provides the equivalence between the existence of an element a fulfilling specific conditions and the satisfaction of the same conditions by a definable element a'.
conditions: There exists an element 'a' such that p(a) holds and b holds, and a equals a'.
function_body:
theorem exists_eq_right_right : (∃ (a : α), p a ∧ b ∧ a = a') ↔ p a' ∧ b := by
  simp [← and_assoc]

name: exists_eq_right_right'
description: This tool asserts the equivalence between the propositions (∃a∈α. pa∧b∧a′=a) and (pa′∧b). It verifies that both conditions provide the same logical outcome.
conditions: ∃ a∈α such that pa ∧ b ∧ a' = a
conclusions: (∃ a∈α. pa ∧ b ∧ a' = a) ↔ (pa' ∧ b)
function_body:
theorem exists_eq_right_right' : (∃ (a : α), p a ∧ b ∧ a' = a) ↔ p a' ∧ b := by
  (conv in _=_ => rw [eq_comm]); simp

name: exists_prop
description: A tool that encapsulates the equivalence between the existence of a conjunction of propositions and the conjunction itself.
function_body: theorem exists_prop : (∃ _h : a, b) ↔ a ∧ b := ⟨fun ⟨hp, hq⟩ => ⟨hp, hq⟩, fun ⟨hp, hq⟩ => ⟨hp, hq⟩⟩

name: exists_apply_eq_apply
description: This tool finds an element 'a' in domain 'α' such that applying function 'f' to 'a' equals applying 'f' to a given element 'a' in the same domain, and shows that 'a' and 'a'' are equal.
conclusions: There exists an element a ∈ α such that f(a) = f(a') and a = a'
function_body: theorem exists_apply_eq_apply (f : α → β) (a' : α) : ∃ a, f a = f a' := ⟨a', rfl⟩

name: forall_prop_of_true
description: This tool proves that if we have a proposition p and a predicate q that holds for p, then q holds for all instances where p is true
function_body:
theorem forall_prop_of_true {p : Prop} {q : p → Prop} (h : p) : (∀ h' : p, q h') ↔ q h :=
  @forall_const (q h) p ⟨h⟩

name: forall_comm
description: A tool that establishes the equivalence between the universal quantification of a predicate p over all pairs (a, b) and (b, a).
conditions: Predicate p(a, b) for all a and b
Predicate p(b, a) for all b and a
conclusions: p(a, b) holds for all a and b if and only if p(b, a) holds for all b and a
function_body:
theorem forall_comm {p : α → β → Prop} : (∀ a b, p a b) ↔ (∀ b a, p a b) :=
  ⟨fun h b a => h a b, fun h a b => h b a⟩

name: exists_comm
description: This tool verifies that the existence of a pair (a, b) such that p(a, b) holds is equivalent to the existence of a pair (b, a) such that p(b, a) holds.
conditions: A predicate p(a, b) on elements a and b of types α and β respectively.
conclusions: The existence of (a, b) such that p(a, b) is equivalent to the existence of (b, a) such that p(b, a).
function_body: theorem exists_comm {p : α → β → Prop} : (∃ a b, p a b) ↔ (∃ b a, p a b) := ⟨fun ⟨a, b, h⟩ => ⟨b, a, h⟩, fun ⟨b, a, h⟩ => ⟨a, b, h⟩⟩

name: forall_apply_eq_imp_iff
description: This tool provides a logical equivalence between two specific formulations of predicates applied through a function.
conditions: There exists a function f : α → β.
There exists a predicate p : β → Prop.
For all a and b, if f a = b then p b.
function_body:
theorem forall_apply_eq_imp_iff {f : α → β} {p : β → Prop} :
(∀ b a, f a = b → p b) ↔ ∀ a, p (f a) := by simp [forall_comm]

name: forall_eq_apply_imp_iff
description: A tool that establishes the equivalence between a property applied to a function's output for all inputs and a property applied directly to all inputs.
conditions: f is a function from a to b
p is a proposition from b to Prop
conclusions: The statement 'for all b and a, if b equals f of a, then p of b' is equivalent to 'for all a, p of f a.'
function_body:
theorem forall_eq_apply_imp_iff {f : α → β} {p : β → Prop} :
(∀ b a, b = f a → p b) ↔ ∀ a, p (f a) := by simp [forall_comm]

name: forall_apply_eq_imp_iff₂
description: This tool provides an equivalence between two logically equivalent statements involving a function and propositions over its domain and codomain.
conclusions: For all b, a, if p(a) then f(a) = b implies q(b) is equivalent to For all a, if p(a) then q(f(a))
function_body: theorem forall_apply_eq_imp_iff₂ {f : α → β} {p : α → Prop} {q : β → Prop} : (∀ b a, p a → f a = b → q b) ↔ ∀ a, p a → q (f a) := ⟨fun h a ha => h (f a) a ha rfl, fun h _ a ha hb => hb ▸ h a ha⟩

name: Decidable.not_not
description: This tool states that if a statement is not false, then it is true. It encapsulates the logical principle that ¬¬p is equivalent to p for a decidable proposition.
function_body: theorem Decidable.not_not [Decidable p] : ¬¬p ↔ p := ⟨of_not_not, not_not_intro⟩

name: Decidable.by_contra
description: This tool provides a mechanism to conclude that a proposition 'p' is true if assuming 'not p' leads to a contradiction.
conditions: Assuming ¬p results in a contradiction (¬p → False)
function_body: theorem Decidable.by_contra [Decidable p] : (¬p → False) → p := of_not_not

name: decide_eq_true_iff
description: This tool verifies the equivalence between the result of the decide function called on a proposition and the truth status of the proposition itself.
conclusions: decide p = true if and only if p is true
function_body: theorem decide_eq_true_iff (p : Prop) [Decidable p] : (decide p = true) ↔ p := by simp

name: decide_eq_false_iff_not
description: This theorem establishes a bi-conditional relationship between a decidable proposition 'p' and its negation based on the outcome of the 'decide' function.
function_body:
theorem decide_eq_false_iff_not (p : Prop) [Decidable p] : (decide p = false) ↔ ¬p :=
  ⟨of_decide_eq_false, decide_eq_false⟩

name: decide_eq_decide
description: A theorem describing the equivalence between two propositions p and q in terms of their decision procedures returning the same result.
conclusions: The decision procedures for p and q return the same result if and only if p is equivalent to q
function_body:
theorem decide_eq_decide {p q : Prop} [Decidable p] [Decidable q] :
    decide p = decide q ↔ (p ↔ q) :=
  ⟨fun h => by rw [← decide_eq_true_iff p, h, decide_eq_true_iff], fun h => by simp [h]⟩

name: Decidable.of_not_imp
description: A tool that determines the truth of 'a' given the knowledge that 'a does not imply b'.
conditions: You know that a does not imply b.
You know that b is not true.
function_body:
theorem Decidable.of_not_imp [Decidable a] (h : ¬(a → b)) : a :=
  byContradiction (not_not_of_not_imp h)

name: Decidable.not_imp_symm
description: This tool proves that if the implication not a implies b holds and b is false, then a must be true.
function_body:
theorem Decidable.not_imp_symm [Decidable a] (h : ¬a → b) (hb : ¬b) : a :=
  byContradiction <| hb ∘ h

name: Decidable.not_imp_comm
description: A tool that shows the logical equivalence between the implications a → b and ¬b → ¬a.
function_body:
theorem Decidable.not_imp_comm [Decidable a] [Decidable b] : (¬a → b) ↔ (¬b → a) :=
  ⟨not_imp_symm, not_imp_symm⟩

name: Decidable.not_imp_self
description: This theorem states that for a proposition a, the statement (¬a → a) is logically equivalent to a.
conditions: The proposition a must be decidable.
function_body:
theorem Decidable.not_imp_self [Decidable a] : (¬a → a) ↔ a := by
  have := @imp_not_self (¬a); rwa [not_not] at this

name: Decidable.or_iff_not_imp_left
description: This tool demonstrates the logical equivalence between 'a or b' and '(not a) implies b' for a decidable proposition a.
conclusions: "a or b" is equivalent to "(not a) implies b"
function_body:
theorem Decidable.or_iff_not_imp_left [Decidable a] : a ∨ b ↔ (¬a → b) :=
  ⟨Or.resolve_left, fun h => dite _ .inl (.inr ∘ h)⟩

name: Decidable.or_iff_not_imp_right
description: This tool demonstrates the equivalence between the disjunction of two propositions and the implication involving the negation of one proposition.
conditions: For any propositions a and b
conclusions: a ∨ b is equivalent to ¬b → a
function_body:
theorem Decidable.or_iff_not_imp_right [Decidable b] : a ∨ b ↔ (¬b → a) :=
or_comm.trans or_iff_not_imp_left

name: Decidable.not_imp_not
description: This tool demonstrates that if ¬(A implies B) is true then B implies A.
function_body:
theorem Decidable.not_imp_not [Decidable a] : (¬a → ¬b) ↔ (b → a) :=
⟨fun h hb => byContradiction (h · hb), mt⟩

name: Nat.sub_sub_self
description: This tool proves that if m is less than or equal to n, then subtracting the difference (n - m) from n yields m.
function_body:
theorem sub_sub_self {n m : Nat} (h : m ≤ n) : n - (n - m) = m :=
  (Nat.sub_eq_iff_eq_add (Nat.sub_le ..)).2 (Nat.add_sub_of_le h).symm

name: Nat.sub_add_comm
description: This tool provides a way to rearrange the terms in a specific arithmetic expression involving natural numbers, ensuring the order of operations respects the subtraction and addition properties under given conditions.
conditions: n, m, k are natural numbers
conclusions: n + m - k = n - k + m
function_body:
theorem sub_add_comm {n m k : Nat} (h : k ≤ n) : n + m - k = n - k + m := by
  rw [Nat.sub_eq_iff_eq_add (Nat.le_trans h (Nat.le_add_right ..))]
  rwa [Nat.add_right_comm, Nat.sub_add_cancel]

name: Nat.sub_one_sub_lt
description: This tool demonstrates that if an integer i is less than another integer n, then the expression n - 1 - i is also less than n.
function_body:
theorem sub_one_sub_lt (h : i < n) : n - 1 - i < n := by
  rw [Nat.sub_sub]
  apply Nat.sub_lt (Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le (Nat.zero_lt_succ _) h)
  rw [Nat.add_comm]; apply Nat.zero_lt_succ

name: Nat.sub_lt_self
description: A tool to prove that if a and b are natural numbers with a < b, then b - a is less than b.
function_body:
theorem sub_lt_self {a b : Nat} (h₀ : 0 < a) (h₁ : a ≤ b) : b - a < b := by
  apply sub_lt _ h₀
  apply Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le h₀ h₁

name: Nat.add_sub_cancel'
description: This tool proves that if m is less than or equal to n for natural numbers m and n, then adding m to the difference (n - m) yields n.
conditions: m and n are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem add_sub_cancel' {n m : Nat} (h : m ≤ n) : m + (n - m) = n := by
  rw [Nat.add_comm, Nat.sub_add_cancel h]

name: Nat.add_le_of_le_sub_left
description: This tool checks if the sum of two natural numbers m and n is less than or equal to k, given that m is less than or equal to k and n is less than or equal to k minus m.
function_body:
theorem add_le_of_le_sub_left {n k m : Nat} (H : m ≤ k) (h : n ≤ k - m) : m + n ≤ k :=
  Nat.not_lt.1 fun h' => Nat.not_lt.2 h (Nat.sub_lt_left_of_lt_add H h')

name: Nat.le_sub_iff_add_le
description: This tool encapsulates the proof that for natural numbers x, y, and k, where k is less than or equal to y, the inequality x ≤ y - k is equivalent to x + k ≤ y.
conditions: x, y, and k are natural numbers
conclusions: x ≤ y - k if and only if x + k ≤ y
function_body:
theorem le_sub_iff_add_le {x y k : Nat} (h : k ≤ y) : x ≤ y - k ↔ x + k ≤ y := by
  rw [← Nat.add_sub_cancel x k, Nat.sub_le_sub_iff_right h, Nat.add_sub_cancel]

name: Nat.sub_le_iff_le_add
description: This tool provides a theorem that relates the subtraction and addition inequalities for natural numbers. It states that for all natural numbers a, b, c, the inequality a - b ≤ c holds if and only if a ≤ c + b.
conditions: a, b, and c are natural numbers
conclusions: a - b ≤ c if and only if a ≤ c + b
function_body:
theorem sub_le_iff_le_add {a b c : Nat} : a - b ≤ c ↔ a ≤ c + b :=
  ⟨Nat.le_add_of_sub_le, sub_le_of_le_add⟩

name: Nat.sub_le_iff_le_add'
description: This theorem states that the condition a - b ≤ c is equivalent to a ≤ b + c, allowing transformations between these inequalities.
conditions: a, b, and c are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem sub_le_iff_le_add' {a b c : Nat} : a - b ≤ c ↔ a ≤ b + c := by
  rw [Nat.sub_le_iff_le_add, Nat.add_comm]

name: Nat.sub_le_sub_iff_left
description: This tool provides a proof for the theorem which states that for natural numbers, if n is less than or equal to k, then k - m is less than or equal to k - n if and only if n is less than or equal to m.
conclusions: k - m ≤ k - n if and only if n ≤ m
function_body:
theorem sub_le_sub_iff_left {n m k : Nat} (hn : n ≤ k) : k - m ≤ k - n ↔ n ≤ m := by refine ⟨fun h => ?_, Nat.sub_le_sub_left _⟩
rwa [Nat.sub_le_iff_le_add', ← Nat.add_sub_assoc hn,
le_sub_iff_add_le (Nat.le_trans hn (Nat.le_add_left ..)),
Nat.add_comm, Nat.add_le_add_iff_right] at h

name: Nat.sub_add_lt_sub
description: This tool states that for natural numbers n, m, and k, if the sum of m and k is less than or equal to n and k is positive, then n minus the sum of m and k is less than n minus m.
function_body:
theorem sub_add_lt_sub {n m k : Nat} (h₁ : m + k ≤ n) (h₂ : 0 < k) : n - (m + k) < n - m :=
  match k with
  | zero => Nat.lt_irrefl _ h₂ |>.elim
  | succ _ =>
    Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le
      (pred_lt (Nat.ne_of_lt $ Nat.sub_pos_of_lt $ lt_of_succ_le h₁).symm)
      (Nat.sub_le_sub_left _ $ Nat.le_add_right ..)

name: Nat.le_min
description: This tool provides a theorem that establishes the equivalence between a natural number being less than or equal to the minimum of two other natural numbers and it being less than or equal to each of those two numbers individually.
conditions: a, b, and c are natural numbers
conclusions: a ≤ min(b, c) if and only if a ≤ b and a ≤ c
function_body:
theorem le_min {a b c : Nat} : a ≤ min b c ↔ a ≤ b ∧ a ≤ c :=
  ⟨fun h => ⟨Nat.le_trans h (Nat.min_le_left ..), Nat.le_trans h (Nat.min_le_right ..)⟩,
   fun ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ => by rw [Nat.min_def]; split <;> assumption⟩

name: Nat.lt_min
description: A tool to determine the equivalence between 'a is less than the minimum of b and c' and 'a is less than both b and c' for natural numbers.
conditions: a, b, c are natural numbers
conclusions: a < min(b, c) ↔ a < b ∧ a < c
function_body: theorem lt_min {a b c : Nat} : a < min b c ↔ a < b ∧ a < c := Nat.le_min

name: Nat.min_eq_left
description: This tool formalizes the theorem that if you have two natural numbers a and b, and a is less than or equal to b, then the minimum of a and b is a.
function_body: theorem min_eq_left {a b : Nat} (h : a ≤ b) : min a b = a := by simp [Nat.min_def, h]

name: Nat.min_eq_right
description: This tool proves that given two natural numbers a and b, if b is less than or equal to a, then the minimum of a and b is b.
function_body:
theorem min_eq_right {a b : Nat} (h : b ≤ a) : min a b = b := by
  rw [Nat.min_comm a b]; exact Nat.min_eq_left h

name: Nat.zero_min
description: This tool provides a theorem that proves the minimum of 0 and any natural number is 0.
conclusions: The minimum of 0 and a natural number is 0
function_body: theorem zero_min (a : Nat) : min 0 a = 0 := Nat.min_eq_left (zero_le a)

name: Positive_Int_Operation
description: A tool that computes the value of a * b where a * b = a^b + b^a for positive integers a and b.
conditions: a and b must be positive integers
function_body: def positive_int_operation (a b : Nat) (h₀ : 0 < a ∧ 0 < b) : Nat := a^b + b^a

name: Nat.max_le
description: This tool verifies the equivalence between the maximum of two natural numbers being less than or equal to a third number, and each of the two numbers individually being less than or equal to the third number.
function_body:
theorem max_le {a b c : Nat} : max a b ≤ c ↔ a ≤ c ∧ b ≤ c :=
  ⟨fun h => ⟨Nat.le_trans (Nat.le_max_left ..) h, Nat.le_trans (Nat.le_max_right ..) h⟩,
   fun ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ => by rw [Nat.max_def]; split <;> assumption⟩

name: Nat.max_eq_right
description: This tool proves that for any two natural numbers a and b, if a is less than or equal to b, then the maximum of a and b is b.
conditions: a and b are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem max_eq_right {a b : Nat} (h : a ≤ b) : max a b = b := by
  simp [Nat.max_def, h, Nat.not_lt.2 h]

name: Nat.max_eq_left
description: A tool to prove that for natural numbers a and b, if b is less than or equal to a, then the maximum of a and b is a.
function_body:
theorem max_eq_left {a b : Nat} (h : b ≤ a) : max a b = a := by
  rw [← Nat.max_comm b a]; exact Nat.max_eq_right h

name: Nat.min_succ_succ
description: This tool calculates the minimum of the successors of two natural numbers and shows that it is equal to the successor of the minimum of the two original numbers.
function_body:
theorem min_succ_succ (x y : Nat) : min (succ x) (succ y) = succ (min x y) := by
  simp [Nat.min_def, succ_le_succ_iff]; split <;> rfl

name: Nat.sub_eq_sub_min
description: A theorem that states for all natural numbers n and m, the expression n - m is equal to n - min(n, m).
conditions: The natural numbers n and m
function_body:
theorem sub_eq_sub_min (n m : Nat) : n - m = n - min n m := by
  rw [Nat.min_def]; split
  · rw [Nat.sub_eq_zero_of_le ‹n ≤ m›, Nat.sub_self]
  · rfl

name: Nat.sub_add_min_cancel
description: This theorem states that for any natural numbers n and m, the expression n - m + min(n, m) is equal to n.
conditions: n and m are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem sub_add_min_cancel (n m : Nat) : n - m + min n m = n := by
  rw [sub_eq_sub_min, Nat.sub_add_cancel (Nat.min_le_left n m)]

name: Nat.sub_add_eq_max
description: This tool verifies that for any two natural numbers a and b, the expression a - b + b equals the maximum of a and b.
conclusions: a - b + b equals max(a, b)
function_body:
theorem sub_add_eq_max {a b : Nat} : a - b + b = max a b := by
  match a.le_total b with
  | .inl hl => rw [Nat.max_eq_right hl, Nat.sub_eq_zero_iff_le.mpr hl, Nat.zero_add]
  | .inr hr => rw [Nat.max_eq_left hr, Nat.sub_add_cancel hr]

name: Nat.mul_right_comm
description: This theorem states that the product of three natural numbers remains unchanged regardless of the order in which the numbers are multiplied, provided the usual properties of multiplication such as associativity and commutativity hold for natural numbers.
conditions: n, m, and k are natural numbers
Multiplication is both associative and commutative
conclusions: n * m * k = n * k * m
function_body:
theorem mul_right_comm (n m k : Nat) : n * m * k = n * k * m := by
  rw [Nat.mul_assoc, Nat.mul_comm m, ← Nat.mul_assoc]

name: Nat.mul_mul_mul_comm
description: This theorem demonstrates the commutative property of multiplication over four natural numbers, showing that the product of their pairwise products can be rearranged.
conditions: a, b, c, and d are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem mul_mul_mul_comm (a b c d : Nat) : (a * b) * (c * d) = (a * c) * (b * d) := by
  rw [Nat.mul_assoc, Nat.mul_assoc, Nat.mul_left_comm b]

name: Nat.mul_two
description: A theorem proving that multiplying any natural number by 2 yields the same result as adding the number to itself.
function_body: theorem mul_two (n : Nat) : n * 2 = n + n := by simp [Nat.mul_succ]

name: Nat.two_mul
description: A tool that proves for any natural number n, 2 * n equals n + n by using mathematical induction.
function_body: theorem two_mul (n : Nat) : 2 * n = n + n := by simp [Nat.succ_mul]

name: Nat.mul_eq_zero
description: A theorem stating that the multiplication of two natural numbers results in zero if and only if at least one of the numbers is zero.
function_body:
theorem mul_eq_zero {n m : Nat} : n * m = 0 ↔ n = 0 ∨ m = 0 :=
  ⟨fun h => match n, m, h with
    | 0,   m, _ => .inl rfl
    | n+1, m, h => by rw [succ_mul] at h; exact .inr (Nat.eq_zero_of_add_eq_zero_left h),
   fun | .inl h | .inr h => by simp [h]⟩

name: Nat.mul_ne_zero_iff
description: This tool verifies that the product of two integers is non-zero if and only if both integers themselves are non-zero.
function_body: theorem mul_ne_zero_iff : n * m ≠ 0 ↔ n ≠ 0 ∧ m ≠ 0 := by simp [mul_eq_zero, not_or]

name: Nat.mul_ne_zero
description: This tool proves that the product of two nonzero natural numbers is nonzero.
conditions: n is a nonzero natural number
m is a nonzero natural number
function_body:
theorem mul_ne_zero (n0 : n ≠ 0) (m0 : m ≠ 0) : n * m ≠ 0 :=
  Nat.mul_ne_zero_iff.2 ⟨n0, m0⟩

name: Nat.mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left
