description: This tool verifies that if 'a' is less than or equal to 'b' and 'c' is a non-negative integer, then multiplying both 'a' and 'b' by 'c' preserves the less-than-or-equal relationship.
function_body:
theorem mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left {a b c : Nat} (h₁ : a ≤ b) : c * a ≤ c * b := by
  if hba : b ≤ a then simp [Nat.le_antisymm hba h₁] else
  if hc0 : c ≤ 0 then simp [Nat.le_antisymm hc0 (zero_le c), Nat.zero_mul] else
  exact Nat.le_of_lt (Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left (Nat.not_le.1 hba) (Nat.not_le.1 hc0))

name: Nat.mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right
description: This tool verifies that if one integer is less than or equal to another, and a nonnegative integer is multiplied by both, the inequality is preserved.
function_body:
theorem mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right {a b c : Nat} (h₁ : a ≤ b) : a * c ≤ b * c := by
  if hba : b ≤ a then simp [Nat.le_antisymm hba h₁] else
  if hc0 : c ≤ 0 then simp [Nat.le_antisymm hc0 (zero_le c), Nat.mul_zero] else
  exact Nat.le_of_lt (Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_right (Nat.not_le.1 hba) (Nat.not_le.1 hc0))

name: Nat.mul_lt_mul
description: This theorem states that if a is less than c, b is less than or equal to d, and b is positive, then the product of a and b is less than the product of c and d.
function_body:
theorem mul_lt_mul (hac : a < c) (hbd : b ≤ d) (pos_b : 0 < b) : a * b < c * d :=
  Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le (Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_right hac pos_b) (Nat.mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hbd)

name: Nat.mul_lt_mul'
description: This tool asserts that under certain conditions involving inequalities between integers and a positive integer, the product of two numbers will be less than the product of another two numbers.
function_body:
theorem mul_lt_mul' (h1 : a ≤ c) (h2 : b < d) (h3 : 0 < c) : a * b < c * d :=
  Nat.lt_of_le_of_lt (Nat.mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right h1) (Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left h2 h3)

name: Nat.succ_mul_succ_eq
description: This theorem states that for any natural numbers a and b, the product of their successors is equal to the sum of their product, a, b, and 1.
function_body:
theorem succ_mul_succ_eq (a b : Nat) : succ a * succ b = a * b + a + b + 1 := by
  rw [mul_succ, succ_mul, Nat.add_right_comm _ a]; rfl

name: Nat.mul_self_sub_mul_self_eq
description: This theorem states that for all natural numbers a and b, the difference of their squares is equal to the product of the sum and the difference of the numbers.
function_body:
theorem mul_self_sub_mul_self_eq (a b : Nat) : a * a - b * b = (a + b) * (a - b) := by
  rw [Nat.mul_sub_left_distrib, Nat.right_distrib, Nat.right_distrib,
      Nat.mul_comm b a, Nat.add_comm (a*a) (a*b), Nat.add_sub_add_left]

name: Nat.mod_add_div
description: A theorem that demonstrates the relationship between the modulo operation and integer division for natural numbers.
function_body:
theorem mod_add_div (m k : Nat) : m % k + k * (m / k) = m := by
  induction m, k using mod.inductionOn with rw [div_eq, mod_eq]
  | base x y h => simp [h]
  | ind x y h IH => simp [h]; rw [Nat.mul_succ, ← Nat.add_assoc, IH, Nat.sub_add_cancel h.2]

name: Nat.div_one
description: This tool proves that for any natural number n, dividing n by 1 results in n.
conclusions: n divided by 1 is equal to n
function_body:
theorem div_one (n : Nat) : n / 1 = n := by
  have := mod_add_div n 1
  rwa [mod_one, Nat.zero_add, Nat.one_mul] at this

name: Nat.div_zero
description: This theorem defines that for any integer n, dividing by zero results in zero by convention, as division by zero is not inherently defined.
function_body: theorem div_zero (n : Nat) : n / 0 = 0 := by rw [div_eq]; simp [Nat.lt_irrefl]

name: Nat.zero_div
description: Proves that the division of zero by any natural number results in zero.
function_body:
theorem zero_div (b : Nat) : 0 / b = 0 :=
  (div_eq 0 b).trans <| if_neg <| And.rec Nat.not_le_of_gt

name: Nat.le_div_iff_mul_le
description: This theorem states that for any positive integer k and any integers x and y, the inequality x ≤ y / k is equivalent to x * k ≤ y. It provides a way to convert between the division form and the multiplication form of inequalities involving integer division.
conclusions: x ≤ y / k ↔ x * k ≤ y
function_body:
theorem le_div_iff_mul_le (k0 : 0 < k) : x ≤ y / k ↔ x * k ≤ y := by
  induction y, k using mod.inductionOn generalizing x with
    (rw [div_eq]; simp [h]; cases x with | zero => simp [zero_le] | succ x => ?_)
  | base y k h =>
    simp [not_succ_le_zero x, succ_mul, Nat.add_comm]
    refine Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le ?_ (Nat.le_add_right ..)
    exact Nat.not_le.1 fun h' => h ⟨k0, h'⟩
  | ind y k h IH =>
    rw [← add_one, Nat.add_le_add_iff_right, IH k0, succ_mul,
        ← Nat.add_sub_cancel (x*k) k, Nat.sub_le_sub_iff_right h.2, Nat.add_sub_cancel]

name: Nat.div_le_of_le_mul
description: This tool provides a theorem that states if a number m is less than or equal to k times another number n, then m divided by k is less than or equal to n.
function_body:
theorem div_le_of_le_mul {m n : Nat} : ∀ {k}, m ≤ k * n → m / k ≤ n
  | 0, _ => by simp [Nat.div_zero, n.zero_le]
  | succ k, h => by
    suffices succ k * (m / succ k) ≤ succ k * n from
      Nat.le_of_mul_le_mul_left this (zero_lt_succ _)
    have h1 : succ k * (m / succ k) ≤ m % succ k + succ k * (m / succ k) := Nat.le_add_left _ _
    have h2 : m % succ k + succ k * (m / succ k) = m := by rw [mod_add_div]
    have h3 : m ≤ succ k * n := h
    rw [← h2] at h3
    exact Nat.le_trans h1 h3

name: Nat.div_eq_sub_div
description: This theorem relates the division of two positive integers a and b, where a is greater than or equal to b, showing that a / b is equal to (a - b) / b + 1.
conditions: a and b are positive integers
function_body:
theorem div_eq_sub_div (h₁ : 0 < b) (h₂ : b ≤ a) : a / b = (a - b) / b + 1 := by
 rw [div_eq a, if_pos]; constructor <;> assumption

name: Nat.div_eq_of_lt
description: This tool proves that if one natural number is less than another, then the result of the division of the first number by the second is zero.
function_body:
theorem div_eq_of_lt (h₀ : a < b) : a / b = 0 := by
  rw [div_eq a, if_neg]
  intro h₁
  apply Nat.not_le_of_gt h₀ h₁.right

name: Nat.div_lt_iff_lt_mul
description: This tool provides the equivalence between the divisibility properties of integers when involving multiplication and division.
conclusions: x / k < y if and only if x < y * k
function_body:
theorem div_lt_iff_lt_mul (Hk : 0 < k) : x / k < y ↔ x < y * k := by
  rw [← Nat.not_le, ← Nat.not_le]; exact not_congr (le_div_iff_mul_le Hk)

name: Nat.sub_mul_div
description: A theorem to show that for natural numbers x, n, and p where n*p ≤ x, the expression (x - n*p) / n equals x / n - p
conditions: x, n, and p are natural numbers
conclusions: (x - n * p) / n = x / n - p
function_body:
theorem sub_mul_div (x n p : Nat) (h₁ : n*p ≤ x) : (x - n*p) / n = x / n - p := by
  match eq_zero_or_pos n with
  | .inl h₀ => rw [h₀, Nat.div_zero, Nat.div_zero, Nat.zero_sub]
  | .inr h₀ => induction p with
    | zero => rw [Nat.mul_zero, Nat.sub_zero, Nat.sub_zero]
    | succ p IH =>
      have h₂ : n * p ≤ x := Nat.le_trans (Nat.mul_le_mul_left _ (le_succ _)) h₁
      have h₃ : x - n * p ≥ n := by
        apply Nat.le_of_add_le_add_right
        rw [Nat.sub_add_cancel h₂, Nat.add_comm]
        rw [mul_succ] at h₁
        exact h₁
      rw [sub_succ, ← IH h₂, div_eq_sub_div h₀ h₃]
      simp [add_one, Nat.pred_succ, mul_succ, Nat.sub_sub]

name: Nat.div_mul_le_self
description: This theorem states that for any two natural numbers m and n, if n is not zero, the product of the integer division of m by n and n is less than or equal to m.
conditions: n = 0 implies m / n is undefined
function_body:
theorem div_mul_le_self : ∀ (m n : Nat), m / n * n ≤ m
  | m, 0   => by simp
  | m, n+1 => (le_div_iff_mul_le (Nat.succ_pos _)).1 (Nat.le_refl _)

name: Nat.add_div_right
description: For any natural number x and any natural number z greater than 0, this tool proves that (x + z) / z = (x / z) + 1.
conditions: z is a natural number greater than 0
function_body:
theorem add_div_right (x : Nat) {z : Nat} (H : 0 < z) : (x + z) / z = succ (x / z) := by
  rw [div_eq_sub_div H (Nat.le_add_left _ _), Nat.add_sub_cancel]

name: Nat.add_div_left
description: This tool proves that the sum of a number and another positive number divided by the latter is equal to one plus the quotient of the first number and the latter.
function_body:
theorem add_div_left (x : Nat) {z : Nat} (H : 0 < z) : (z + x) / z = succ (x / z) := by
  rw [Nat.add_comm, add_div_right x H]

name: Nat.mul_div_right
description: This theorem proves that for natural numbers m and n, where m is positive, the result of m multiplied by n divided by m is equal to n.
conditions: m and n are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem mul_div_right (n : Nat) {m : Nat} (H : 0 < m) : m * n / m = n := by
  induction n <;> simp_all [mul_succ]

name: Nat.mul_div_left
description: This tool proves that for any natural numbers m and n, given n is greater than 0, m multiplied by n divided by n is equal to m.
function_body:
theorem mul_div_left (m : Nat) {n : Nat} (H : 0 < n) : m * n / n = m := by
  rw [Nat.mul_comm, mul_div_right _ H]

name: Nat.div_self
description: A theorem stating that any positive integer divided by itself is equal to 1.
function_body:
theorem div_self (H : 0 < n) : n / n = 1 := by
  let t := add_div_right 0 H
  rwa [Nat.zero_add, Nat.zero_div] at t

name: Nat.add_mul_div_left
description: This tool provides a proof by induction that for all natural numbers x, y, and z, where y is nonzero, the equation (x + y * z) / y = x / y + z holds.
conditions: x, y, and z are natural numbers
conclusions: (x + y * z) / y = x / y + z
function_body:
theorem add_mul_div_left (x z : Nat) {y : Nat} (H : 0 < y) : (x + y * z) / y = x / y + z := by
  induction z with
  | zero => rw [Nat.mul_zero, Nat.add_zero, Nat.add_zero]
  | succ z ih => rw [mul_succ, ← Nat.add_assoc, add_div_right _ H, ih]; rfl

name: Nat.add_mul_div_right
description: This tool verifies that for natural numbers x, y, and z where z is greater than zero, the expression (x + y * z) / z simplifies to x / z + y.
conclusions: (x + y * z) / z = x / z + y
function_body:
theorem add_mul_div_right (x y : Nat) {z : Nat} (H : 0 < z) : (x + y * z) / z = x / z + y := by
  rw [Nat.mul_comm, add_mul_div_left _ _ H]

name: Nat.mul_div_cancel
description: This tool shows that for any natural number n greater than 0, dividing m times n by n yields m.
function_body:
theorem mul_div_cancel (m : Nat) {n : Nat} (H : 0 < n) : m * n / n = m := by
  let t := add_mul_div_right 0 m H
  rwa [Nat.zero_add, Nat.zero_div, Nat.zero_add] at t

name: Nat.mul_div_cancel_left
description: This tool proves that for any positive integers n and m, the expression n * m / n simplifies to m.
function_body:
theorem mul_div_cancel_left (m : Nat) {n : Nat} (H : 0 < n) : n * m / n = m :=
by rw [Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_div_cancel _ H]

name: Nat.div_eq_of_eq_mul_left
description: This tool proves that if m = k * n and n > 0 for natural numbers m, n, and k, then m divided by n equals k.
function_body: theorem div_eq_of_eq_mul_left (H1 : 0 < n) (H2 : m = k * n) : m / n = k := by rw [H2, Nat.mul_div_cancel _ H1]

name: Nat.div_eq_of_eq_mul_right
description: This theorem states that if a natural number m is the product of n and k, and n is greater than zero, then the division of m by n equals k.
function_body:
theorem div_eq_of_eq_mul_right (H1 : 0 < n) (H2 : m = n * k) : m / n = k :=
by rw [H2, Nat.mul_div_cancel_left _ H1]

name: Nat.div_eq_of_lt_le
description: This tool provides a formal proof that if an integer m lies between kn and (k+1)n, then the integer division of m by n equals k.
function_body:
theorem div_eq_of_lt_le (lo : k * n ≤ m) (hi : m < succ k * n) : m / n = k :=
have npos : 0 < n := (eq_zero_or_pos _).resolve_left fun hn => by
  rw [hn, Nat.mul_zero] at hi lo; exact absurd lo (Nat.not_le_of_gt hi)
Nat.le_antisymm
  (le_of_lt_succ ((Nat.div_lt_iff_lt_mul npos).2 hi))
  ((Nat.le_div_iff_mul_le npos).2 lo)

name: Nat.mul_sub_div
description: This theorem demonstrates the relationship between division and subtraction for natural numbers under certain conditions. Specifically, it shows how a subtraction inside a quotient can be rewritten to match a specific form.
function_body:
theorem mul_sub_div (x n p : Nat) (h₁ : x < n*p) : (n * p - succ x) / n = p - succ (x / n) := by
  have npos : 0 < n := (eq_zero_or_pos _).resolve_left fun n0 => by
    rw [n0, Nat.zero_mul] at h₁; exact not_lt_zero _ h₁
  apply Nat.div_eq_of_lt_le
  · rw [Nat.mul_sub_right_distrib, Nat.mul_comm]
    exact Nat.sub_le_sub_left _ <| (div_lt_iff_lt_mul npos).1 (lt_succ_self _)
  · show succ (pred (n * p - x)) ≤ (succ (pred (p - x / n))) * n
    rw [succ_pred_eq_of_pos (Nat.sub_pos_of_lt h₁),
      fun h => succ_pred_eq_of_pos (Nat.sub_pos_of_lt h)] -- TODO: why is the function needed?
    · rw [Nat.mul_sub_right_distrib, Nat.mul_comm]
      exact Nat.sub_le_sub_left _ <| div_mul_le_self ..
    · rwa [div_lt_iff_lt_mul npos, Nat.mul_comm]

name: Nat.div_div_eq_div_mul
description: This theorem states that for positive integers m, n, and k, the result of dividing m by n/k is equal to the result of dividing m by the product of n and k.
conditions: m, n, and k are positive integers
function_body:
theorem div_div_eq_div_mul (m n k : Nat) : m / n / k = m / (n * k) := by
  cases eq_zero_or_pos k with
  | inl k0 => rw [k0, Nat.mul_zero, Nat.div_zero, Nat.div_zero] | inr kpos => ?_
  cases eq_zero_or_pos n with
  | inl n0 => rw [n0, Nat.zero_mul, Nat.div_zero, Nat.zero_div] | inr npos => ?_
  apply Nat.le_antisymm
  · apply (le_div_iff_mul_le (Nat.mul_pos npos kpos)).2
    rw [Nat.mul_comm n k, ← Nat.mul_assoc]
    apply (le_div_iff_mul_le npos).1
    apply (le_div_iff_mul_le kpos).1
    (apply Nat.le_refl)
  · apply (le_div_iff_mul_le kpos).2
    apply (le_div_iff_mul_le npos).2
    rw [Nat.mul_assoc, Nat.mul_comm n k]
    apply (le_div_iff_mul_le (Nat.mul_pos kpos npos)).1
    apply Nat.le_refl

name: Nat.mul_div_mul_left
description: This tool states and proves that for all natural numbers m, n, and k, where m is positive, the fraction (m * n) / (m * k) simplifies to n / k.
conditions: m is a positive natural number
n and k are natural numbers
function_body: theorem mul_div_mul_left {m : Nat} (n k : Nat) (H : 0 < m) : m * n / (m * k) = n / k := by rw [← Nat.div_div_eq_div_mul, Nat.mul_div_cancel_left _ H]

name: Nat.mul_div_mul_right
description: This tool proves that for natural numbers n, m, and k with m > 0, the expression (n * m) / (k * m) simplifies to n / k.
conditions: n, m, k are natural numbers
function_body: theorem mul_div_mul_right {m : Nat} (n k : Nat) (H : 0 < m) : n * m / (k * m) = n / k := by rw [Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_comm k, Nat.mul_div_mul_left _ _ H]

name: Nat.mul_div_le
description: This tool proves that for any natural numbers m and n, with n positive, n times the quotient of m divided by n is less than or equal to m.
function_body:
theorem mul_div_le (m n : Nat) : n * (m / n) ≤ m := by
  match n, Nat.eq_zero_or_pos n with
  | _, Or.inl rfl => rw [Nat.zero_mul]; exact m.zero_le
  | n, Or.inr h => rw [Nat.mul_comm, ← Nat.le_div_iff_mul_le h]; exact Nat.le_refl _

name: Nat.mod_two_eq_zero_or_one
description: This tool proves that for any natural number n, the result of n modulo 2 is either 0 or 1.
function_body:
theorem mod_two_eq_zero_or_one (n : Nat) : n % 2 = 0 ∨ n % 2 = 1 :=
  match n % 2, @Nat.mod_lt n 2 (by simp) with
  | 0, _ => .inl rfl
  | 1, _ => .inr rfl

name: Nat.le_of_mod_lt
description: This theorem states that if the remainder of the division of a natural number 'a' by a natural number 'b' is less than 'a', then 'b' must be less than or equal to 'a'.
conditions: a and b are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem le_of_mod_lt {a b : Nat} (h : a % b < a) : b ≤ a :=
  Nat.not_lt.1 fun hf => (ne_of_lt h).elim (Nat.mod_eq_of_lt hf)

name: Nat.add_mod_right
description: This theorem states that for any natural numbers x and z, adding z to x and then taking the modulo z operation yields the same result as just taking x modulo z.
function_body:
theorem add_mod_right (x z : Nat) : (x + z) % z = x % z := by
  rw [mod_eq_sub_mod (Nat.le_add_left ..), Nat.add_sub_cancel]

name: Nat.add_mod_left
description: A tool that proves for any natural numbers x and z, (x + z) mod x equals z mod x.
function_body:
theorem add_mod_left (x z : Nat) : (x + z) % x = z % x := by
  rw [Nat.add_comm, add_mod_right]

name: Nat.add_mul_mod_self_left
description: This theorem shows that for any natural numbers x, y, and z, the expression (x + y * z) modulo y equals x modulo y.
function_body:
theorem add_mul_mod_self_left (x y z : Nat) : (x + y * z) % y = x % y := by
  match z with
  | 0 => rw [Nat.mul_zero, Nat.add_zero]
  | succ z => rw [mul_succ, ← Nat.add_assoc, add_mod_right, add_mul_mod_self_left (z := z)]

name: Nat.add_mul_mod_self_right
description: This theorem states that for any natural numbers x, y, and z, the modulus of x added to y times z with respect to z is equal to the modulus of x with respect to z.
function_body:
theorem add_mul_mod_self_right (x y z : Nat) : (x + y * z) % z = x % z := by
  rw [Nat.mul_comm, add_mul_mod_self_left]

name: Nat.mul_mod_right
description: This tool proves that the product of any two natural numbers, when divided by the first number, leaves a remainder of zero.
function_body:
theorem mul_mod_right (m n : Nat) : (m * n) % m = 0 := by
  rw [← Nat.zero_add (m * n), add_mul_mod_self_left, zero_mod]

name: Nat.mul_mod_left
description: This theorem states that for any natural numbers m and n, the product of m and n modulo n is always 0.
function_body:
theorem mul_mod_left (m n : Nat) : (m * n) % n = 0 := by
  rw [Nat.mul_comm, mul_mod_right]

name: Nat.mul_mod_mul_left
description: This theorem states that for all natural numbers z, x, and y, if y and z are non-zero, then (z * x) % (z * y) is equal to z * (x % y).
function_body:
theorem mul_mod_mul_left (z x y : Nat) : (z * x) % (z * y) = z * (x % y) :=
  if y0 : y = 0 then by
    rw [y0, Nat.mul_zero, mod_zero, mod_zero]
  else if z0 : z = 0 then by
    rw [z0, Nat.zero_mul, Nat.zero_mul, Nat.zero_mul, mod_zero]
  else by
    induction x using Nat.strongInductionOn with
    | _ n IH =>
      have y0 : y > 0 := Nat.pos_of_ne_zero y0
      have z0 : z > 0 := Nat.pos_of_ne_zero z0
      cases Nat.lt_or_ge n y with
      | inl yn => rw [mod_eq_of_lt yn, mod_eq_of_lt (Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left yn z0)]
      | inr yn =>
        rw [mod_eq_sub_mod yn, mod_eq_sub_mod (Nat.mul_le_mul_left z yn),
          ← Nat.mul_sub_left_distrib]
        exact IH _ (sub_lt (Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le y0 yn) y0)

name: Nat.mul_mod_mul_right
description: This theorem states that for natural numbers x, y, and z, multiplying x by z and taking the modulus with y multiplied by z gives the same result as taking x modulo y and then multiplying by z.
conditions: x, y, and z are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem mul_mod_mul_right (z x y : Nat) : (x * z) % (y * z) = (x % y) * z := by
  rw [Nat.mul_comm x z, Nat.mul_comm y z, Nat.mul_comm (x % y) z]; apply mul_mod_mul_left

name: Nat.sub_mul_mod
description: A theorem stating that if n * k ≤ x, then (x - n * k) % n is equal to x % n.
function_body:
theorem sub_mul_mod {x k n : Nat} (h₁ : n*k ≤ x) : (x - n*k) % n = x % n := by
  match k with
  | 0 => rw [Nat.mul_zero, Nat.sub_zero]
  | succ k =>
    have h₂ : n * k ≤ x := Nat.le_trans (le_add_right _ n) h₁
    have h₄ : x - n * k ≥ n := by
      apply Nat.le_of_add_le_add_right (b := n * k)
      rw [Nat.sub_add_cancel h₂]
      simp [mul_succ, Nat.add_comm] at h₁; simp [h₁]
    rw [mul_succ, ← Nat.sub_sub, ← mod_eq_sub_mod h₄, sub_mul_mod h₂]

name: Nat.mod_mod
description: This tool demonstrates that taking the remainder of an already processed remainder does not change the result; that is, (a % n) % n = a % n.
function_body:
theorem mod_mod (a n : Nat) : (a % n) % n = a % n :=
  match eq_zero_or_pos n with
  | .inl n0 => by simp [n0, mod_zero]
  | .inr npos => Nat.mod_eq_of_lt (mod_lt _ npos)

name: Nat.mul_mod
description: This theorem provides a way to compute the modulo of the product of two natural numbers efficiently by leveraging the modulo of each operand individually.
conditions: a, b, and n are natural numbers
conclusions: a * b % n = (a % n) * (b % n) % n
function_body:
theorem mul_mod (a b n : Nat) : a * b % n = (a % n) * (b % n) % n := by
 conv => lhs;
 rw [
  ← mod_add_div a n, ← mod_add_div b n, Nat.add_mul, Nat.mul_add, Nat.mul_add,
  Nat.mul_assoc, Nat.mul_assoc, ← Nat.mul_add n, add_mul_mod_self_left,
  Nat.mul_comm _ (n * (b / n)), Nat.mul_assoc, add_mul_mod_self_left]

name: Nat.mod_add_mod
description: A theorem stating that the remainder of m divided by n plus k is equal to the remainder of m plus k divided by n.
function_body:
theorem mod_add_mod (m n k : Nat) : (m % n + k) % n = (m + k) % n := by
  have := (add_mul_mod_self_left (m % n + k) n (m / n)).symm
  rwa [Nat.add_right_comm, mod_add_div] at this

name: Nat.add_mod_mod
description: This theorem states that for all natural numbers m, n, and k, the result of adding m to the remainder of n divided by k, then taking the remainder of the result divided by k is equal to the result of adding m and n, then taking the remainder divided by k.
function_body:
theorem add_mod_mod (m n k : Nat) : (m + n % k) % k = (m + n) % k := by
  rw [Nat.add_comm, mod_add_mod, Nat.add_comm]

name: Nat.add_mod
description: This theorem states that the modulo of a sum of two natural numbers is equal to the modulo of the sum of their individual modulos, when taken with respect to the same natural number.
conditions: a, b, and n are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem add_mod (a b n : Nat) : (a + b) % n = ((a % n) + (b % n)) % n := by
  rw [add_mod_mod, mod_add_mod]

name: Nat.pow_succ'
description: This tool verifies the definition of exponentiation, particularly the property that raising a number to the (n+1)th power is equivalent to multiplying the number by its nth power.
conditions: m and n are natural numbers
Exponentiation and multiplication are defined for these numbers
function_body:
theorem pow_succ' {m n : Nat} : m ^ n.succ = m * m ^ n := by
  rw [Nat.pow_succ, Nat.mul_comm]

name: Nat.pow_eq
description: This tool proves that the infix operator `pow` defined in Lean4 for natural numbers is equivalent to the standard exponentiation operator `^` in mathematics.
conclusions: m.pow n is equal to m ^ n
function_body: theorem pow_eq {m n : Nat} : m.pow n = m ^ n := rfl

name: Nat.shiftLeft_eq
description: This theorem proves that the left shift operation on natural numbers is equivalent to multiplication by a power of 2.
function_body:
theorem shiftLeft_eq (a b : Nat) : a <<< b = a * 2 ^ b :=
  match b with
  | 0 => (Nat.mul_one _).symm
  | b+1 => (shiftLeft_eq _ b).trans <| by
    simp [pow_succ, Nat.mul_assoc, Nat.mul_left_comm, Nat.mul_comm]

name: Nat.one_shiftLeft
description: This tool proves that shifting the number 1 left by any natural number n results in the value 2 raised to the power of n.
conclusions: 1 shifted left by n equals 2 raised to the power of n
function_body: theorem one_shiftLeft (n : Nat) : 1 <<< n = 2 ^ n := by rw [shiftLeft_eq, Nat.one_mul]

name: Nat.zero_pow
description: This tool proves that for any natural number n > 0, raising 0 to the power of n results in 0.
function_body:
theorem zero_pow {n : Nat} (H : 0 < n) : 0 ^ n = 0 := by
  match n with
  | 0 => contradiction
  | n+1 => rw [Nat.pow_succ, Nat.mul_zero]

name: Nat.one_pow
description: This tool proves that 1 raised to any natural number power is equal to 1.
function_body:
theorem one_pow (n : Nat) : 1 ^ n = 1 := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ _ ih => rw [Nat.pow_succ, Nat.mul_one, ih]

name: Nat.pow_one
description: This tool verifies that raising any natural number 'a' to the power of 1 results in 'a'.
function_body:
theorem pow_one (a : Nat) : a ^ 1 = a := by
  rw [Nat.pow_succ, Nat.pow_zero, Nat.one_mul]

name: Nat.pow_two
description: This tool provides a proof by induction that for any natural number a, the square of a is equal to a multiplied by a.
function_body:
theorem pow_two (a : Nat) : a ^ 2 = a * a :=
  Nat.recOn a
    (by rw [Nat.zero_pow (by decide), Nat.zero_mul])
    (λ n h, by rw [Nat.succ_pow, Nat.pow_one, h, Nat.mul_succ, Nat.succ_mul, h])

name: Nat.pow_add
description: This theorem demonstrates the property of exponentiation where multiplying a base 'a' raised to the sum of two exponents equals the product of the base 'a' raised to each exponent.
conditions: m and n are natural numbers
Exponentiation is defined for base a for all natural numbers
conclusions: a ^ (m + n) = a ^ m * a ^ n
function_body:
theorem pow_add (a m n : Nat) : a ^ (m + n) = a ^ m * a ^ n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rw [Nat.add_zero, Nat.pow_zero, Nat.mul_one]
  | succ _ ih => rw [Nat.add_succ, Nat.pow_succ, Nat.pow_succ, ih, Nat.mul_assoc]

name: Nat.pow_add'
description: This tool proves that raising a natural number to the power of the sum of two other natural numbers is equivalent to multiplying the individual powers of the same base.
function_body:
theorem pow_add' (a m n : Nat) : a ^ (m + n) = a ^ n * a ^ m := by
  rw [←Nat.pow_add, Nat.add_comm]

name: Nat.pow_mul'
description: The tool 'pow_mul'' proves that for any natural numbers a, m, and n, the expression a^(mn) is equivalent to (a^n)^m using the property of exponentiation and mathematical induction.
conditions: m and n are natural numbers.
function_body:
theorem pow_mul' (a m n : Nat) : a ^ (m * n) = (a ^ n) ^ m := by
  rw [←Nat.pow_mul, Nat.mul_comm]

name: Nat.pow_right_comm
description: A theorem that states for all natural numbers a, m, and n, the expression (a^m)^n is equal to (a^n)^m.
conditions: a, m, and n are natural numbers
function_body:
theorem pow_right_comm (a m n : Nat) : (a ^ m) ^ n = (a ^ n) ^ m := by
  rw [←Nat.pow_mul, Nat.pow_mul']

name: Nat.mul_pow
description: This tool proves that for any natural numbers a, b, and n, the exponentiation of the product (a * b) raised to the power n is equal to the product of the exponentiations a^n and b^n.
function_body:
theorem mul_pow (a b n : Nat) : (a * b) ^ n = a ^ n * b ^ n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rw [Nat.pow_zero, Nat.pow_zero, Nat.pow_zero, Nat.mul_one]
  | succ _ ih => rw [Nat.pow_succ, Nat.pow_succ, Nat.pow_succ, Nat.mul_mul_mul_comm, ih]

name: Nat.le_log2
description: This theorem states that for any non-zero natural number n and any integer k, k <= log2(n) if and only if 2^k <= n. The proof establishes the contrapositive of each direction.
conditions: n is a natural number and n ≠ 0
conclusions: k ≤ log2(n) if and only if 2^k ≤ n
function_body:
theorem le_log2 (h : n ≠ 0) : k ≤ n.log2 ↔ 2 ^ k ≤ n := by
  match k with
  | 0 => simp [show 1 ≤ n from Nat.pos_of_ne_zero h]
  | k+1 =>
    rw [log2]; split
    · have n0 : 0 < n / 2 := (Nat.le_div_iff_mul_le (by decide)).2 ‹_›
      simp [Nat.add_le_add_iff_right, le_log2 (Nat.ne_of_gt n0), le_div_iff_mul_le, Nat.pow_succ]
    · simp only [le_zero_eq, succ_ne_zero, false_iff]
      refine mt (Nat.le_trans ?_) ‹_›
      exact Nat.pow_le_pow_of_le_right (Nat.succ_pos 1) (Nat.le_add_left 1 k)

name: Nat.log2_lt
description: This tool provides a way to establish an equivalence between an inequality involving a positive integer and an inequality involving its logarithm base 2.
conclusions: n < 2^k is equivalent to log2(n) < k
function_body:
theorem log2_lt (h : n ≠ 0) : n.log2 < k ↔ n < 2 ^ k := by
  rw [← Nat.not_le, ← Nat.not_le, le_log2 h]

name: Nat.log2_self_le
description: This theorem proves that for any positive integer n, the value 2 raised to the power of the logarithm base 2 of n is less than or equal to n. This is based on properties of logarithms and the monotonicity of the exponentiation function.
function_body: theorem log2_self_le (h : n ≠ 0) : 2 ^ n.log2 ≤ n := (le_log2 h).1 (Nat.le_refl _)

name: Nat.lt_log2_self
description: This tool proves that any positive integer n is less than 2^(n+1) using properties of logarithms and exponentiation.
function_body: theorem lt_log2_self (h : n ≠ 0) : n < 2 ^ (n.log2 + 1) := (log2_lt h).1 (Nat.le_refl _)

name: Nat.dvd_refl
description: This tool verifies that any natural number n divides itself and that 1 divides any natural number n.
function_body: theorem dvd_refl (a : Nat) : a ∣ a := ⟨1, by simp⟩

name: Order.pred_top_le_iff
description: A theorem that states if the predecessor of an element is less than or equal to the top element, then the element is either the top element or the predecessor of the top element.
function_body:
theorem pred_top_le_iff : pred ⊤ ≤ a ↔ a = ⊤ ∨ a = pred ⊤ :=
  @le_succ_bot_iff αᵒᵈ _ _ _ _

name: Order.pred_lt_top
description: This tool demonstrates that for any element `a` in a well-founded relation that is not the minimum, the predecessor of `a` is strictly smaller than the top element.
conditions: Element `a` is part of a well-founded relation.
conclusions: The predecessor of `a` is strictly smaller than the top element.
function_body:
theorem pred_lt_top (a : α) : pred a < ⊤ :=
  (pred_mono le_top).trans_lt <| pred_lt_of_not_isMin not_isMin_top

name: Order.pred_ne_top
description: A tool that ensures the predecessor of a natural number is not equal to the top element.
conclusions: pred a is not equal to top
function_body:
theorem pred_ne_top (a : α) : pred a ≠ ⊤ :=
  (pred_lt_top a).ne

name: Order.pred_eq_iSup
description: This tool proves that for a given element in a set, its predecessor is equal to the least upper bound of the set of all elements that are less than it.
conditions: The element a belongs to the set α.
There is a defined order on the elements of α.
conclusions: pred a is the largest element in α that is strictly less than a, equal to the least upper bound of all elements in α that are less than a.
function_body:
theorem pred_eq_iSup (a : α) : pred a = ⨆ (b) (_ : b < a), b := by
  refine' le_antisymm _ (iSup_le fun b => iSup_le le_pred_of_lt)
  obtain rfl | ha := eq_or_ne a ⊥
  · rw [pred_bot]
    exact bot_le
  · exact @le_iSup₂ _ _ (fun b => b < a) _ (fun a _ => a) (pred a) (pred_lt_iff_ne_bot.2 ha)

name: Order.succ_pred_of_not_isMin
description: A theorem stating that the successor of the predecessor of a number is equal to the number itself, given that the number is not minimal.
conditions: The number is not minimal (¬IsMin a)
conclusions: The successor of the predecessor of the number is equal to the number (succ (pred a) = a)
function_body:
theorem succ_pred_of_not_isMin (h : ¬IsMin a) : succ (pred a) = a :=
  Covby.succ_eq (pred_covby_of_not_isMin h)

name: Multiplication.zero_result_right
description: If two numbers are multiplied and their product is zero, then if the first number is not zero, the second number must be zero.
function_body:
lemma isZero_of_mul_eq_zero (h : a * b = 0) (ha : a ≠ 0) : b = 0 :=
  by
    -- aesop?
    apply isZero_of_mul_eq_zero_left ha h

name: Order.succ_pred
description: This theorem demonstrates that for any number \( a \), the successor of its predecessor is equal to the number itself.
conditions: The number system utilizes a NoMinOrder α, meaning there is no minimum element.
conclusions: For any number \( a \), \( succ(pred(a)) = a \).
function_body:
theorem succ_pred [NoMinOrder α] (a : α) : succ (pred a) = a :=
  Covby.succ_eq (pred_covby _)

name: Order.pred_succ
description: This tool proves that the predecessor of the successor of any natural number is the original number by using mathematical induction.
function_body:
theorem pred_succ [NoMaxOrder α] (a : α) : pred (succ a) = a :=
  Covby.pred_eq (covby_succ _)

name: Order.pred_succ_iterate_of_not_isMax
description: This theorem states that if an element i is not a maximal element in a well-founded partial order, then iterating the predecessor function n times on the result of iterating the successor function n times on i will result in i.
conditions: i is an element of a well-founded partial order A
i is not a maximal element in A
function_body:
theorem pred_succ_iterate_of_not_isMax (i : α) (n : ℕ) (hin : ¬IsMax (succ^[n - 1] i)) : pred^[n] (succ^[n] i) = i := by
  induction' n with n hn
  · simp only [Nat.zero_eq, Function.iterate_zero, id.def]
  rw [Nat.succ_sub_succ_eq_sub, Nat.sub_zero] at hin
  have h_not_max : ¬IsMax (succ^[n - 1] i) := by
    cases' n with n
    · simpa using hin
    rw [Nat.succ_sub_succ_eq_sub, Nat.sub_zero] at hn ⊢
    have h_sub_le : succ^[n] i ≤ succ^[n.succ] i := by
      rw [Function.iterate_succ']
      exact le_succ _
    refine' fun h_max => hin fun j hj => _
    have hj_le : j ≤ succ^[n] i := h_max (h_sub_le.trans hj)
    exact hj_le.trans h_sub_le
  rw [Function.iterate_succ, Function.iterate_succ']
  simp only [Function.comp_apply]
  rw [pred_succ_of_not_isMax hin]
  exact hn h_not_max

name: Order.succ_pred_iterate_of_not_isMin
description: This tool shows that the `n`th successor of the `n`th predecessor of a value `i` in a discrete type `α` is equal to `i`, given that `i` is not the minimal value of `α`.
conditions: i is a value in a discrete type α.
n is a natural number greater than 0.
i is not the minimal value of α.
conclusions: The `n`th successor of the `n`th predecessor of `i` is equal to `i`.

name: WithTop.succ_coe_top
description: A theorem stating that the successor of the top element in the type α is equal to the top element in the WithTop α structure.
conditions: α is a type that has a top element (⊤)
function_body:
theorem succ_coe_top : succ ↑(⊤ : α) = (⊤ : WithTop α) :=
  dif_pos rfl

name: WithTop.succ_coe_of_ne_top
description: This theorem states that for an element 'a' of type α that is not equal to the top element, the successor of 'a' in the type with top element is equal to the successor of 'a' in the type without top element.
conditions: a is an element of type α
a is not equal to the top element (a ≠ ⊤)
conclusions: The successor of a in WithTop α is equal to the successor of a in α
function_body:
theorem succ_coe_of_ne_top {a : α} (h : a ≠ ⊤) : succ (↑a : WithTop α) = ↑(succ a) :=
  dif_neg h

name: WithTop.pred_top
description: This tool shows that the predecessor of the top element in the WithTop type is the top element when lifted into the WithTop type.
conditions: ⊤ is the top element of WithTop α
function_body:
theorem pred_top : pred (⊤ : WithTop α) = ↑(⊤ : α) :=
  rfl

name: WithTop.pred_coe
description: This theorem shows that in a set with a top element, the predecessor of the coercion of an element is equivalent to the coercion of the predecessor of the element.
conditions: Existence of a set with a top element
A coercion function that maps an element to its corresponding element in the set with a top element
function_body:
theorem pred_coe (a : α) : pred (↑a : WithTop α) = ↑(pred a) :=
  rfl

name: WithTop.pred_untop
description: A theorem that describes the relationship between the predecessor of the untop of a non-top element and the untop of the predecessor of that element.
conditions: a is an element of a type that has a top element
a is not the top element
conclusions: The predecessor of a.untop is equal to the untop of the predecessor of a
function_body:
theorem pred_untop :
    ∀ (a : WithTop α) (ha : a ≠ ⊤),
      pred (a.untop ha) = (pred a).untop (by induction a using WithTop.recTopCoe <;> simp)
  | ⊤, ha => (ha rfl).elim
  | (a : α), _ => rfl

name: WithTop.succ_coe
description: A tool to show that applying the successor function to a value of type `α` with a `WithTop` structure is equivalent to applying the successor function after coercing the value to `WithTop α`.
conditions: For a type `α` with a `WithTop` structure.
conclusions: Applying `succ` to a value `a` of type `α` is the same as applying `succ` to `a` after coercing it to `WithTop α`.
function_body:
theorem succ_coe (a : α) : succ (↑a : WithTop α) = ↑(succ a) :=
  rfl

name: WithBot.succ_bot
description: This tool encapsulates the theorem that the successor of the bottom element (⊥) in a sequence is the bottom element (⊥) itself.
conditions: Succ function is defined within a sequence with a well-defined bottom (⊥) element.
function_body:
theorem succ_bot : succ (⊥ : WithBot α) = ↑(⊥ : α) :=
  rfl

name: WithBot.succ_coe
description: This tool demonstrates that for an element a of type α, the successor of its lift to WithBot is equal to the lift of its successor.
conditions: a is an element of type α.
function_body:
theorem succ_coe (a : α) : succ (↑a : WithBot α) = ↑(succ a) :=
  rfl

name: WithBot.succ_unbot
description: A theorem that states that the successor of the unbot of an element a, where a is not equal to the bottom element, is the unbot of the successor of a.
function_body: theorem succ_unbot : ∀ (a : WithBot α) (ha : a ≠ ⊥), succ (a.unbot ha) = (succ a).unbot (by induction a using WithBot.recBotCoe <;> simp) | ⊥, ha => (ha rfl).elim | (a : α), _ => rfl

name: WithBot.pred_coe_bot
description: A tool that ensures the predecessor of the least element in a type extended with a bottom element (WithBot) is also the least element.
conditions: α is a type with a least element (⊥).
pred is a function that maps elements of α to their predecessors.
function_body:
theorem pred_coe_bot : pred ↑(⊥ : α) = (⊥ : WithBot α) :=
  dif_pos rfl

name: WithBot.pred_coe_of_ne_bot
description: This theorem proves that if a non-bottom element is lifted to a WithBot type, the predecessor of the lifted element is equivalent to lifting the predecessor of the original element.
conditions: Let a: α be a non-bottom element (a ≠ ⊥).
function_body:
theorem pred_coe_of_ne_bot {a : α} (h : a ≠ ⊥) : pred (↑a : WithBot α) = ↑(pred a) :=
  dif_neg h

name: WithBot.pred_coe
description: A tool for proving that for a type with decidable equality, the predecessor of an injected value into WithBot is the injected predecessor of that value
function_body: theorem pred_coe (a : α) : pred (↑a : WithBot α) = ↑(pred a) := rfl

name: exists_succ_iterate_iff_le
description: This theorem states that for all real numbers a and b, there exists a natural number n such that iterating the successor function n times to a equals b if and only if a is less than or equal to b.
conditions: a and b are real numbers
conclusions: There exists a natural number n such that a + n = b if and only if a ≤ b
function_body:
theorem exists_succ_iterate_iff_le : (∃ n, succ^[n] a = b) ↔ a ≤ b := by
  refine' ⟨_, exists_succ_iterate_of_le⟩
  rintro ⟨n, rfl⟩
  exact id_le_iterate_of_id_le le_succ n a

name: Succ.rec
description: A theorem that uses induction to prove that a property `P` holds for all elements greater than or equal to a specified element `m`, given that `P` holds for `m` and that `P` is preserved under the successor function.
conditions: For any element `n` greater than or equal to `m`, if `P` holds for `n`, then `P` holds for the successor of `n`.
conclusions: Property `P` holds for all elements greater than or equal to `m`.
function_body:
theorem Succ.rec {P : α → Prop} {m : α} (h0 : P m) (h1 : ∀ n, m ≤ n → P n → P (succ n)) ⦃n : α⦄
(hmn : m ≤ n) : P n := by
  obtain ⟨n, rfl⟩ := hmn.exists_succ_iterate; clear hmn
  induction' n with n ih
  · exact h0
  · rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply']
    exact h1 _ (id_le_iterate_of_id_le le_succ n m) ih

name: Succ.rec_iff
description: A tool to determine that a property P is true for all natural numbers if it is true for a given number and its successor.
conditions: Property P holds for a given natural number
Property P holds for the successor of each natural number where it holds
conclusions: Property P holds for all natural numbers
function_body:
theorem Succ.rec_iff {p : α → Prop} (hsucc : ∀ a, p a ↔ p (succ a)) {a b : α} (h : a ≤ b) :
    p a ↔ p b := by
  obtain ⟨n, rfl⟩ := h.exists_succ_iterate
  exact Iterate.rec (fun b => p a ↔ p b) (fun c hc => hc.trans (hsucc _)) Iff.rfl n

name: LE.le.exists_pred_iterate
description: Given two elements a and b in a linearly ordered set with a ≤ b, this theorem guarantees the existence of a natural number n such that subtracting n from b (interpreted as iterating a predecessor operation n times on b) results in a.
conditions: a and b are elements of a linearly ordered set
conclusions: There exists a natural number n such that pred^[n] b = a
function_body:
theorem LE.le.exists_pred_iterate (h : a ≤ b) : ∃ n, pred^[n] b = a :=
  exists_pred_iterate_of_le h

name: exists_pred_iterate_iff_le
description: This theorem proves that if there exists an element n such that the n-th predecessor iterate of b equals a in an ordered set, then a is less than or equal to b.
function_body:
theorem exists_pred_iterate_iff_le : (∃ n, pred^[n] b = a) ↔ a ≤ b :=
  @exists_succ_iterate_iff_le αᵒᵈ _ _ _ _ _

name: Pred.rec
description: This tool performs induction on a predicate P over elements less than or equal to m, ensuring that if P holds for m and for pred(n) given P(n), then P holds for all n <= m.
conditions: For all n <= m, if P(n) holds, then P(pred(n)) holds.
conclusions: For all n <= m, P(n) holds.

name: Pred.rec_iff
description: Shows that a propositional function holds for all natural numbers if it holds for the base case and the inductive step.
conditions: For all x, if p(x) holds, then p(x+1) holds
conclusions: p(x) holds for all natural numbers x
function_body:
theorem Pred.rec_iff {p : α → Prop} (hsucc : ∀ a, p a ↔ p (pred a)) {a b : α} (h : a ≤ b) :
    p a ↔ p b :=
  (@Succ.rec_iff αᵒᵈ _ _ _ _ hsucc _ _ h).symm

name: exists_succ_iterate_or
description: This tool determines that for any two natural numbers a and b, either there is an n such that the nth successor of a equals b, or there is an n such that the nth successor of b equals a.
conclusions: There exists a natural number n such that the nth successor of a is b, or there exists a natural number n such that the nth successor of b is a
function_body:
theorem exists_succ_iterate_or : (∃ n, succ^[n] a = b) ∨ ∃ n, succ^[n] b = a :=
  (le_total a b).imp exists_succ_iterate_of_le exists_succ_iterate_of_le

name: Succ.rec_linear
description: This tool provides a theorem that demonstrates if a propositional function on a type α holds for an element a if and only if it holds for its successor, then it holds for any two elements a and b within α.
conditions: p is a propositional function on a type α
hsucc states that p(a) ↔ p(succ a)
conclusions: p(a) ↔ p(b) for any a, b in α
function_body:
theorem Succ.rec_linear {p : α → Prop} (hsucc : ∀ a, p a ↔ p (succ a)) (a b : α) : p a ↔ p b :=
  (le_total a b).elim (Succ.rec_iff hsucc) fun h => (Succ.rec_iff hsucc h).symm

name: exists_pred_iterate_or
description: This tool determines whether one integer can be transformed into another by repeatedly applying the predecessor function, ensuring that for any two integers, either one can be reached from the other.
conclusions: (∃ n, pred^[n] b = a) ∨ (∃ n, pred^[n] a = b)
function_body: theorem exists_pred_iterate_or : (∃ n, pred^[n] b = a) ∨ ∃ n, pred^[n] a = b := (le_total a b).imp exists_pred_iterate_of_le exists_pred_iterate_of_le

name: Pred.rec_linear
description: This tool proves that for elements a and b of a well-ordered set with a predecessor operation, if a property holds for a, it also holds for b under certain conditions.
conditions: a and b are elements of a well-ordered set with a predecessor operation
p is a property on elements of the set
If p holds for an element, it also holds for its predecessor
conclusions: If a has property p, then b also has property p
function_body:
theorem Pred.rec_linear {p : α → Prop} (hsucc : ∀ a, p a ↔ p (pred a)) (a b : α) : p a ↔ p b :=
  (le_total a b).elim (Pred.rec_iff hsucc) fun h => (Pred.rec_iff hsucc h).symm

name: StrictMono.not_bddAbove_range
description: A tool to prove that a strictly increasing function from a set ordered by a non-maximum order to a set ordered by a successor order, which is also a successor Archimedean order, has a range that is not bounded above.
conditions: f is a strictly increasing function (StrictMono f)
The domain of f is a set ordered by a non-maximum order (NoMaxOrder α)
The codomain of f is ordered by a successor order (SuccOrder β)
The codomain is a successor Archimedean order (IsSuccArchimedean β)
conclusions: The range of f is not bounded above (¬ BddAbove (Set.range f))
function_body:
lemma StrictMono.not_bddAbove_range [NoMaxOrder α] [SuccOrder β] [IsSuccArchimedean β] (hf : StrictMono f) : ¬ BddAbove (Set.range f) := by
  rintro ⟨m, hm⟩
  have hm' : ∀ a, f a ≤ m := λ a ↦ hm $ Set.mem_range_self _
  obtain ⟨a₀⟩ := ‹Nonempty α›
  suffices ∀ b, f a₀ ≤ b → ∃ a, b < f a by
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ : ∃ a, m < f a := this m (hm' a₀)
    exact ha.not_le (hm' a)
  have h : ∀ a, ∃ a', f a < f a' := λ a ↦ (exists_gt a).imp (λ a' h ↦ hf h)
  apply Succ.rec
  · exact h a₀
  rintro b _ ⟨a, hba⟩
  exact (h a).imp (λ a' ↦ (succ_le_of_lt hba).trans_lt)

name: StrictMono.not_bddBelow_range
description: This tool proves that if a function f is strictly monotonic, then the range of f is not bounded below.
conclusions: The range of f is not bounded below
function_body: lemma StrictMono.not_bddBelow_range [NoMinOrder α] [PredOrder β] [IsPredArchimedean β] (hf : StrictMono f) : ¬ BddBelow (Set.range f) := hf.dual.not_bddAbove_range

name: StrictAnti.not_bddAbove_range
description: This tool proves that the range of a strictly antitone function from a successor ordinal to a well-ordered set with no minimum element is not bounded above.
conditions: α is a well-ordered set with no minimum element
f: β → α is a strictly antitone function
conclusions: The range of f is not bounded above
function_body:
lemma StrictAnti.not_bddAbove_range [NoMinOrder α] [SuccOrder β] [IsSuccArchimedean β]
(hf : StrictAnti f) : ¬ BddAbove (Set.range f) := hf.dual_right.not_bddBelow_range

name: StrictAnti.not_bddBelow_range
description: This tool encapsulates the lemma stating that if a function is strictly antitone, then its range is not bounded below.
conclusions: The range of f is not bounded below
function_body: lemma StrictAnti.not_bddBelow_range [NoMaxOrder α] [PredOrder β] [IsPredArchimedean β] (hf : StrictAnti f) : ¬ BddBelow (Set.range f) := hf.dual_right.not_bddAbove_range

name: Subset_emptyset_implies_empty
description: A theorem that states any set that is a subset of the empty set must be the empty set.
function_body:
theorem Subset_emptyset_implies_empty {α : Type*} (A : set α) (h : A ⊆ ∅) : A = ∅ :=
  eq_empty_iff_forall_not_mem.mpr (λ x hx, not_mem_empty x (h hx))

name: Pred.rec_top
description: The predicate recursor for a top type `α` provides a way to determine the truth value of a predicate on any element of the type, given the truth value at the top element and a method to propagate the truth value backwards through predecessors.
conditions: A top type `α` with a least element `⊤`.
A base case `htop` that gives the truth value of the predicate at `⊤`.
A recursive case `hpred` that propagates the truth value of the predicate from an element to its predecessor.
conclusions: The truth value of the predicate `p` at any element `a` in the type `α`.
function_body:
theorem Pred.rec_top (p : α → Prop) (htop : p ⊤) (hpred : ∀ a, p a → p (pred a)) (a : α) : p a :=
  Pred.rec htop (fun x _ h => hpred x h) (le_top : a ≤ ⊤)

name: SuccOrder.forall_ne_bot_iff
description: This tool provides a means to prove that a property P holds for all non-bottom elements in a partially ordered set with a bottom element, an order successor, and the successor Archimedean property, if and only if P holds for all successors of elements.
conditions: The set is a partially ordered set.
The set has a bottom element.
There exists an order successor for every element in the set.
The set satisfies the successor Archimedean property.
conclusions: P holds for all non-bottom elements if and only if P holds for all successors of elements.
function_body:
lemma SuccOrder.forall_ne_bot_iff
    [Nontrivial α] [PartialOrder α] [OrderBot α] [SuccOrder α] [IsSuccArchimedean α]
    (P : α → Prop) :
    (∀ i, i ≠ ⊥ → P i) ↔ (∀ i, P (SuccOrder.succ i)) := by
  refine' ⟨fun h i ↦ h _ (Order.succ_ne_bot i), fun h i hi ↦ _⟩
  obtain ⟨j, rfl⟩ := exists_succ_iterate_of_le (bot_le : ⊥ ≤ i)
  have hj : 0 < j := by apply Nat.pos_of_ne_zero; contrapose! hi; simp [hi]
  rw [← Nat.succ_pred_eq_of_pos hj]
  simp only [Function.iterate_succ', Function.comp_apply]
  apply h

name: Neighborhood.zero_continuousAtPoint
description: This tool proves that a function f is continuous at a point a if f(x) = 0 in a neighborhood of a in a topological space.
conditions: f(x) = 0 for all x in a neighborhood of a
function_body:
theorem zero_continuousAtPoint {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] {f : X -> ℝ} {a : X} (h : ∃ U : set X, U ∈ 𝓝 a ∧ ∀ x ∈ U, f x = 0) : ContinuousAt f a :=
  begin
    rw continuous_at,
    intros N hN,
    rcases h with ⟨U, hU₁, hU₂⟩,
    use [U, hU₁],
    intros x hx,
    rw hU₂ x hx,
    exact hN,
  end

name: Filter.ZeroAtFilter.add
description: This tool shows that if two functions, f and g, both tend to zero at a filter l, then their sum f+g also tends to zero at the same filter l.
conditions: f tends to 0 at filter l
g tends to 0 at filter l
conclusions: f+g tends to 0 at filter l
function_body:
theorem ZeroAtFilter.add [TopologicalSpace β] [AddZeroClass β] [ContinuousAdd β] {l : Filter α} {f g : α → β} (hf : ZeroAtFilter l f) (hg : ZeroAtFilter l g) : ZeroAtFilter l (f + g) := by
  simpa using hf.add hg

name: Filter.ZeroAtFilter.neg
description: This tool provides the theorem stating that if a function f converges to zero at a given filter, then the negation of that function, -f, also converges to zero at the same filter.
conditions: f converges to zero at a filter l
conclusions: -f converges to zero at the same filter l
function_body: theorem ZeroAtFilter.neg [TopologicalSpace β] [AddGroup β] [ContinuousNeg β] {l : Filter α} {f : α → β} (hf : ZeroAtFilter l f) : ZeroAtFilter l (-f) := by simpa using hf.neg

name: Filter.ZeroAtFilter.smul
description: This tool proves that if a function f is zero at a filter l, then multiplying f by a scalar c in a topological space 𝕜 results in a function that is also zero at the same filter l.
conditions: 𝕜 is a type with a topological space and a zero element
β is a type with a topological space and a zero element
l is a filter on α
f is a function from α to β
f is zero at filter l, denoted as ZeroAtFilter l f
conclusions: The function c • f is zero at filter l
function_body: theorem ZeroAtFilter.smul {𝕜 : Type*} [TopologicalSpace 𝕜] [TopologicalSpace β] [Zero 𝕜] [Zero β] [SMulWithZero 𝕜 β] [ContinuousSMul 𝕜 β] {l : Filter α} {f : α → β} (c : 𝕜) (hf : ZeroAtFilter l f) : ZeroAtFilter l (c • f) := by simpa using hf.const_smul c

name: Filter.ZeroAtFilter.boundedAtFilter
description: This tool verifies that if a function tends to zero at a particular filter, the function is also bounded on that filter.
conditions: A function f(x) tends to zero at a filter L
conclusions: The function f(x) is bounded on the filter L
function_body:
theorem ZeroAtFilter.boundedAtFilter [NormedAddCommGroup β] {l : Filter α} {f : α → β}
    (hf : ZeroAtFilter l f) : BoundedAtFilter l f := by
  rw [ZeroAtFilter, ← Asymptotics.isLittleO_const_iff (one_ne_zero' ℝ)] at hf
  exact hf.isBigO

name: Filter.const_boundedAtFilter
description: This tool proves that a constant function is bounded at every filter using its Lipschitz continuity with constant 0.
conditions: The function in question is a constant function.
The constant function is Lipschitz continuous with constant 0.
conclusions: The constant function is bounded at every filter.
function_body:
theorem const_boundedAtFilter [NormedField β] (l : Filter α) (c : β) : BoundedAtFilter l (Function.const α c : α → β) :=
  Asymptotics.isBigO_const_const c one_ne_zero l

name: Filter.BoundedAtFilter.add
description: This tool demonstrates that if two functions f and g are bounded at a filter l on a set α, then their sum f + g is also bounded at the same filter l.
conditions: f is bounded at filter l.
g is bounded at filter l.
conclusions: f + g is bounded at filter l.

name: Filter.BoundedAtFilter.neg
description: This tool provides a theorem demonstrating that if a function is bounded at a filter, then its negation is also bounded at the same filter.
conditions: l is a filter on a set α.
f: α → β is a bounded function.
conclusions: -f is also a bounded function on α.
function_body: theorem BoundedAtFilter.neg [NormedAddCommGroup β] {l : Filter α} {f : α → β} (hf : BoundedAtFilter l f) : BoundedAtFilter l (-f) := hf.neg_left

name: Filter.BoundedAtFilter.mul
description: This tool states that if two functions are bounded at a filter, their pointwise product is also bounded at the same filter.
conditions: A filter l on a set α
Two maps f and g from α to a normed field β
conclusions: The product f * g is bounded at l
function_body:
theorem BoundedAtFilter.mul [NormedField β] {l : Filter α} {f g : α → β}
(hf : BoundedAtFilter l f) (hg : BoundedAtFilter l g) : BoundedAtFilter l (f * g) := by
refine' (hf.mul hg).trans _
convert Asymptotics.isBigO_refl (E := ℝ) _ l
simp

name: Filter.HasBasis.subsingleton_iff
description: This theorem provides the necessary and sufficient conditions under which all sets in a collection indexed by a set are of the same size. Specifically, it states that the sets are all of the same size if and only if there is an index such that the corresponding set is a singleton.
conditions: There is a collection of sets indexed by a set ι.
The sets s_i are all the same size.
conclusions: There is a set i such that i is in ι and s_i is a singleton.
function_body: theorem HasBasis.subsingleton_iff {ι : Sort*} {p : ι → Prop} {s : ι → Set α} (h : l.HasBasis p s) : l.Subsingleton ↔ ∃ i, p i ∧ (s i).Subsingleton := h.exists_iff fun _ _ hsub h ↦ h.anti hsub

name: Filter.Subsingleton.anti
description: This tool proves that if `l` is a subsingleton type, and `l'` is a subtype of `l`, then `l'` is also a subsingleton type.
conditions: l' is a subtype of l
function_body:
theorem Subsingleton.anti {l'} (hl : l.Subsingleton) (hl' : l' ≤ l) : l'.Subsingleton :=
  let ⟨s, hsl, hs⟩ := hl; ⟨s, hl' hsl, hs⟩

name: Filter.Subsingleton.of_subsingleton
description: A theorem stating that if a type is subsingleton, then its list type is also subsingleton.
conclusions: The list type of α is subsingleton.
function_body:
theorem Subsingleton.of_subsingleton [Subsingleton α] : Subsingleton (List α) :=
  by apply_instance

name: Filter.Subsingleton.map
description: This theorem asserts that if a list is a singleton, then mapping any function over this list results in a singleton list.
conditions: The list l is a singleton.
There exists a function f from α to β.
conclusions: The map of the singleton list l by the function f is also a singleton.
function_body:
theorem Subsingleton.map (hl : l.Subsingleton) (f : α → β) : (map f l).Subsingleton :=
  let ⟨s, hsl, hs⟩ := hl; ⟨f '' s, image_mem_map hsl, hs.image f⟩

name: Filter.Subsingleton.prod
description: This theorem states that the Cartesian product of two subsingletons is also a subsingleton.
function_body:
theorem Subsingleton.prod (hl : l.Subsingleton) {l' : Filter β} (hl' : l'.Subsingleton) : (l ×ˢ l').Subsingleton :=
  let ⟨s, hsl, hs⟩ := hl; let ⟨t, htl', ht⟩ := hl'; ⟨s ×ˢ t, prod_mem_prod hsl htl', hs.prod ht⟩

name: Filter.subsingleton_pure
description: This tool proves that the pure filter of a subsingleton set is a subsingleton filter. In other words, if a set contains only one element, then the filter generated by that set contains all sets that include this single element and is a subsingleton.
conditions: S is a subsingleton set with singleton representative 'a'.
conclusions: The pure filter of S is a subsingleton filter.
function_body:
theorem subsingleton_pure {a : α} : Filter.Subsingleton (pure a) :=
  ⟨{a}, rfl, subsingleton_singleton⟩

name: Filter.subsingleton_bot
description: This tool proves that the bottom filter, generated by the empty set, is a subsingleton.
conditions: The concept of filters in a set context
Understanding of the bottom filter being generated by the empty set
conclusions: The bottom filter is a subsingleton
function_body:
theorem subsingleton_bot : Filter.Subsingleton (⊥ : Filter α) :=
  ⟨∅, trivial, subsingleton_empty⟩

name: Filter.Subsingleton.exists_eq_pure
description: This tool proves that for any subsingleton list `l`, there exists an element `a` such that `l` is equal to the pure list containing `a`.
conclusions: There exists an element `a` such that `l` is equal to the pure list containing `a`
function_body:
theorem Subsingleton.exists_eq_pure [l.NeBot] (hl : l.Subsingleton) : ∃ a, l = pure a := by
  rcases hl with ⟨s, hsl, hs⟩
  rcases exists_eq_singleton_iff_nonempty_subsingleton.2 ⟨nonempty_of_mem hsl, hs⟩ with ⟨a, rfl⟩
  refine ⟨a, (NeBot.le_pure_iff ‹_›).1 ?_⟩
  rwa [le_pure_iff]

name: Filter.subsingleton_iff_bot_or_pure
description: This theorem states that a type is subsingleton if and only if it is either empty or a singleton type with exactly one element.
conditions: Type l is empty or non-empty
conclusions: Type l is empty or a singleton type with exactly one element
function_body:
theorem subsingleton_iff_bot_or_pure : l.Subsingleton ↔ l = ⊥ ∨ ∃ a, l = pure a := by
  refine ⟨fun hl ↦ ?_, ?_⟩
  · exact (eq_or_neBot l).imp_right (@Subsingleton.exists_eq_pure _ _ · hl)
  · rintro (rfl | ⟨a, rfl⟩) <;> simp

name: Filter.subsingleton_iff_exists_le_pure
description: A tool that determines if a list is a subsingleton based on the existence of an element that is less than or equal to all other elements in the list.
conditions: The list is either empty or comprises only pure elements
conclusions: There exists an element 'a' such that 'l ≤ pure a'
function_body:
theorem subsingleton_iff_exists_le_pure [Nonempty α] : l.Subsingleton ↔ ∃ a, l ≤ pure a := by
  rcases eq_or_neBot l with rfl | hbot
  · simp
  · simp [subsingleton_iff_bot_or_pure, ← hbot.le_pure_iff, hbot.ne]

name: Filter.subsingleton_iff_exists_singleton_mem
description: A tool that provides a necessary and sufficient condition for a Lean list to be a subsingleton by checking if there is a singleton list within it.
conditions: Any two elements a and b in the list l must satisfy a = b.
conclusions: There exists a unique element a in the list l such that {a} is in l.
function_body:
theorem subsingleton_iff_exists_singleton_mem [Nonempty α] : l.Subsingleton ↔ ∃ a, {a} ∈ l := by
  simp only [subsingleton_iff_exists_le_pure, le_pure_iff]

name: Filter.Subsingleton.isCountablyGenerated
description: This tool proves that a subsingleton type is countably generated. Since every element of a subsingleton type is equivalent to each other, the type is either the bottom type or a singleton, and in either case, it is countably generated.
conditions: The type must be a subsingleton.
function_body:
lemma Subsingleton.isCountablyGenerated (hl : l.Subsingleton) : IsCountablyGenerated l := by
  rcases subsingleton_iff_bot_or_pure.1 hl with rfl|⟨x, rfl⟩
  · exact isCountablyGenerated_bot
  · exact isCountablyGenerated_pure x

name: Nat.comap_cast_atTop
description: This theorem establishes that for a strictly ordered semiring R that is also Archimedean, the comap of the natural-to-real casting function, applied to the at-top element of the reals, equals the at-top element of the naturals. This is based on the embedding properties of the casting function.
conditions: R is a strictly ordered semiring
conclusions: The comap of the function that casts a natural number to a real number, when applied to the at-top element of the reals, is equal to the at-top element of the naturals.
function_body:
theorem Nat.comap_cast_atTop [StrictOrderedSemiring R] [Archimedean R] :
    comap ((↑) : ℕ → R) atTop = atTop :=
  comap_embedding_atTop (fun _ _ => Nat.cast_le) exists_nat_ge

name: tendsto_nat_cast_atTop_iff
description: This theorem establishes the equivalence between a function from a strictly ordered semiring tending to infinity with respect to a filter and its natural number cast function into an Archimedean ordered semiring tending to infinity with respect to the same filter.
conclusions: The function $f$ tends to infinity along filter $l$ if and only if the function $α → R$ given by $x ↦ f(x) : R$ tends to infinity along $l$.
function_body: theorem tendsto_nat_cast_atTop_iff [StrictOrderedSemiring R] [Archimedean R] {f : α → ℕ} {l : Filter α} : Tendsto (fun n => (f n : R)) l atTop ↔ Tendsto f l atTop := tendsto_atTop_embedding (fun _ _ => Nat.cast_le) exists_nat_ge

name: tendsto_nat_cast_atTop_atTop
description: This tool asserts that the natural number casting function f(n) = n, when mapped from natural numbers to real numbers, tends to infinity as n tends to infinity.
conditions: The function f is defined as f(n) = n where n belongs to natural numbers.
The real numbers R form a Dedekind-complete ordered field.
conclusions: The function f(n) = n tends to infinity as n tends to infinity.
function_body: theorem tendsto_nat_cast_atTop_atTop [StrictOrderedSemiring R] [Archimedean R] : Tendsto ((↑) : ℕ → R) atTop atTop := tendsto_nat_cast_atTop_iff.2 tendsto_id

name: Filter.Eventually.nat_cast_atTop
description: This tool proves that if a proposition is eventually true for real numbers, it is also eventually true for natural numbers using the Archimedean property of real numbers.
conditions: p(x) is eventually true for x in ℝ
ℝ is an Archimedean ordered field
conclusions: p(n) is eventually true for n in ℕ
function_body: theorem Filter.Eventually.nat_cast_atTop [StrictOrderedSemiring R] [Archimedean R] {p : R → Prop} (h : ∀ᶠ (x:R) in atTop, p x) : ∀ᶠ (n:ℕ) in atTop, p n := by rw [←Nat.comap_cast_atTop (R := R)]; exact h.comap _

name: Int.comap_cast_atTop
description: A theorem stating that for any strictly ordered and Archimedean ring R, the comap of the integer embedding takes the atTop predicate to itself.
conditions: R is a strictly ordered ring.
conclusions: The comap of the embedding ℤ → R takes atTop to itself.
function_body: theorem Int.comap_cast_atTop [StrictOrderedRing R] [Archimedean R] : comap ((↑) : ℤ → R) atTop = atTop := comap_embedding_atTop (fun _ _ => Int.cast_le) fun r => let ⟨n, hn⟩ := exists_nat_ge r; ⟨n, by exact_mod_cast hn⟩

name: Int.comap_cast_atBot
description: This tool demonstrates that the comap of the cast function from the integers ℤ to a strictly ordered and Archimedean ring R at negative infinity is negative infinity.
conditions: R is a strictly ordered ring
conclusions: The comap of the cast function from ℤ to R at negative infinity is negative infinity
function_body:
theorem Int.comap_cast_atBot [StrictOrderedRing R] [Archimedean R] :
    comap ((↑) : ℤ → R) atBot = atBot :=
  comap_embedding_atBot (fun _ _ => Int.cast_le) fun r =>
    let ⟨n, hn⟩ := exists_nat_ge (-r)
    ⟨-n, by simpa [neg_le] using hn⟩

name: tendsto_int_cast_atTop_iff
description: This tool provides the equivalence of the existence of a limit of a function from a set to the integers at infinity, and the limit existing in the reals.
conditions: f: A -> ℤ is a function
conclusions: lim_{x -> ∞} f(x) exists in ℝ if and only if lim_{x -> ∞} f(x) exists in ℤ
function_body: theorem tendsto_int_cast_atTop_iff [StrictOrderedRing R] [Archimedean R] {f : α → ℤ} {l : Filter α} : Tendsto (fun n => (f n : R)) l atTop ↔ Tendsto f l atTop := by rw [← @Int.comap_cast_atTop R, tendsto_comap_iff]; rfl

name: tendsto_int_cast_atBot_iff
description: This tool determines if a function \( f \) mapping from a set α to the integers goes to negative infinity based on whether the function cast to a strict ordered ring \( R \) tends to negative infinity, using a filter \( l \).
conditions: f is a function from α to ℤ
l is a filter on α
conclusions: If (f → ∞) as α → ∞, then (f → -∞) as α → -∞
function_body: theorem tendsto_int_cast_atBot_iff [StrictOrderedRing R] [Archimedean R] {f : α → ℤ} {l : Filter α} : Tendsto (fun n => (f n : R)) l atBot ↔ Tendsto f l atBot := by rw [← @Int.comap_cast_atBot R, tendsto_comap_iff]; rfl

name: tendsto_int_cast_atTop_atTop
description: This tool proves that the function casting integers to real numbers tends to infinity as the integer argument tends to infinity.
conditions: The function (↑) : ℤ → R is order-preserving
conclusions: The function (↑) : ℤ → R converges to infinity as the integer argument approaches infinity
function_body:
theorem tendsto_int_cast_atTop_atTop [StrictOrderedRing R] [Archimedean R] :
    Tendsto ((↑) : ℤ → R) atTop atTop :=
  tendsto_int_cast_atTop_iff.2 tendsto_id

name: Filter.Eventually.int_cast_atTop
description: This tool asserts that if a property P eventually holds for a strictly ordered, Archimedean ring R as its elements approach infinity, then P eventually holds for integers as the integers approach infinity.
conditions: R is a strictly ordered ring
Property P eventually holds for elements of R as they approach infinity
conclusions: Property P eventually holds for integers as they approach infinity
function_body: theorem Filter.Eventually.int_cast_atTop [StrictOrderedRing R] [Archimedean R] {p : R → Prop} (h : ∀ᶠ (x:R) in atTop, p x) : ∀ᶠ (n:ℤ) in atTop, p n := by rw [←Int.comap_cast_atTop (R := R)]; exact h.comap _

name: Filter.Eventually.int_cast_atBot
description: Given a strictly ordered, Archimedean ring R and a predicate p on R that holds for all values sufficiently close to negative infinity, this theorem guarantees the existence of an integer threshold n such that p holds for all integers less than this threshold.
conditions: R is a strictly ordered ring
p(x) holds for all x sufficiently close to -∞
conclusions: There exists an integer n such that for all m < n, p(m) holds
function_body: theorem Filter.Eventually.int_cast_atBot [StrictOrderedRing R] [Archimedean R] {p : R → Prop} (h : ∀ᶠ (x:R) in atBot, p x) : ∀ᶠ (n:ℤ) in atBot, p n := by rw [←Int.comap_cast_atBot (R := R)]; exact h.comap _

name: Rat.comap_cast_atTop
description: This tool demonstrates that the comap of the embedding from the rationals to an Archimedean ordered field is equal to the top element.
conclusions: comap of the embedding from ℚ to R equals atTop
function_body:
theorem Rat.comap_cast_atTop [LinearOrderedField R] [Archimedean R] :
  comap ((↑) : ℚ → R) atTop = atTop :=
comap_embedding_atTop (fun _ _ => Rat.cast_le) fun r =>
  let ⟨n, hn⟩ := exists_nat_ge r; ⟨n, by simpa⟩

name: Rat.comap_cast_atBot
description: This tool shows that casting a rational number to a real number retains the property that it approaches negative infinity when the rational number does.
conditions: The real numbers are an Archimedean field
We have a linear ordered field R
conclusions: Casting a rational number to a real number as the rational number approaches negative infinity results in the real number approaching negative infinity
function_body:
theorem Rat.comap_cast_atBot [LinearOrderedField R] [Archimedean R] :
    comap ((↑) : ℚ → R) atBot = atBot :=
  comap_embedding_atBot (fun _ _ => Rat.cast_le) fun r =>
    let ⟨n, hn⟩ := exists_nat_ge (-r)
    ⟨-n, by simpa [neg_le] ⟩

name: tendsto_rat_cast_atTop_iff
description: This tool verifies the equivalence of a function tending to infinity and its composition with a rational cast tending to infinity in a given filter on a linear ordered field.
conditions: R is a linear ordered field
l is a filter on α
conclusions: f tends to infinity in the filter l if and only if f ∘ rat_cast tends to infinity in the filter l
function_body: theorem tendsto_rat_cast_atTop_iff [LinearOrderedField R] [Archimedean R] {f : α → ℚ} {l : Filter α} : Tendsto (fun n => (f n : R)) l atTop ↔ Tendsto f l atTop := by rw [← @Rat.comap_cast_atTop R, tendsto_comap_iff]; rfl

name: tendsto_rat_cast_atBot_iff
description: Relates the behavior of a function tending to infinity with the behavior of its reciprocal tending to zero along a filter.
conditions: f: X -> ℚ is a function
l is a filter on X
conclusions: f tends to infinity along l if and only if 1/f tends to zero along l
function_body: theorem tendsto_rat_cast_atBot_iff [LinearOrderedField R] [Archimedean R] {f : α → ℚ} {l : Filter α} : Tendsto (fun n => (f n : R)) l atBot ↔ Tendsto f l atBot := by rw [← @Rat.comap_cast_atBot R, tendsto_comap_iff]; rfl

name: Filter.Eventually.rat_cast_atTop
description: This tool states that if a property holds eventually for real numbers in an archimedean field, then it also holds eventually for the set of rational numbers.
conditions: The field R is a Linear Ordered Field.
The property p eventually holds for real numbers.
conclusions: The property p eventually holds for rational numbers.
function_body: theorem Filter.Eventually.rat_cast_atTop [LinearOrderedField R] [Archimedean R] {p : R → Prop} (h : ∀ᶠ (x:R) in atTop, p x) : ∀ᶠ (n:ℚ) in atTop, p n := by rw [←Rat.comap_cast_atTop (R := R)]; exact h.comap _

name: Filter.Eventually.rat_cast_atBot
description: This tool verifies that if a predicate is eventually true for real numbers, it will also be eventually true for rational numbers.
conditions: The predicate is eventually true of real numbers.
conclusions: The predicate is eventually true of rationals.
function_body: theorem Filter.Eventually.rat_cast_atBot [LinearOrderedField R] [Archimedean R] {p : R → Prop} (h : ∀ᶠ (x:R) in atBot, p x) : ∀ᶠ (n:ℚ) in atBot, p n := by rw [←Rat.comap_cast_atBot (R := R)]; exact h.comap _

name: atTop_hasAntitoneBasis_of_archimedean
description: This tool demonstrates that the filter at the top of an Archimedean ordered semiring has an antitone basis formed by the sets Ici n for all n in ℕ.
conditions: The structure R must be a Strict Ordered Semiring
conclusions: The filter generated by the sets Ici n for all n in ℕ has an antitone basis
function_body:
theorem atTop_hasAntitoneBasis_of_archimedean [StrictOrderedSemiring R] [Archimedean R] :
    (atTop : Filter R).HasAntitoneBasis fun n : ℕ => Ici n where
  antitone := fun _ _ h => Ici_subset_Ici.2 (Nat.mono_cast h)
  mem_iff' _t := ⟨fun ht => iInf_sets_induct ht ⟨0, trivial, subset_univ _⟩
      fun {x _ _} h₁ ⟨n, _, hn⟩ =>
        let ⟨m, hm⟩ := exists_nat_ge x
        ⟨max m n, trivial, fun _y hy => ⟨h₁ (hm.trans ((Nat.cast_le.2 (le_max_left _ _)).trans hy)),
          hn <| (Nat.cast_le.2 (le_max_right _ _)).trans hy⟩⟩,
    fun ⟨_n, _, hn⟩ => mem_of_superset (Ici_mem_atTop _) hn⟩

name: atTop_hasCountableBasis_of_archimedean
description: This tool demonstrates that in a strictly ordered semiring with the Archimedean property, the filter of neighborhoods of the top element has a countable basis.
conclusions: Filter of neighborhoods of the top element has a countable basis
function_body:
theorem atTop_hasCountableBasis_of_archimedean [StrictOrderedSemiring R] [Archimedean R] :
    (atTop : Filter R).HasCountableBasis (fun _ : ℕ => True) fun n => Ici n :=
  ⟨atTop_hasAntitoneBasis_of_archimedean.1, to_countable _⟩

name: atBot_hasCountableBasis_of_archimedean
description: A tool to determine that the filter of sets of the form {x | x < m} in an Archimedean linear ordered ring has a countable basis.
conditions: R is a linear ordered ring
conclusions: The filter of sets of the form {x | x < m} has a countable basis
function_body:
theorem atBot_hasCountableBasis_of_archimedean [LinearOrderedRing R] [Archimedean R] :
    (atBot : Filter R).HasCountableBasis (fun _ : ℤ => True) fun m => Iic m :=
  { countable := to_countable _
    toHasBasis :=
      atBot_basis.to_hasBasis
        (fun x _ => let ⟨m, hm⟩ := exists_int_lt x; ⟨m, trivial, Iic_subset_Iic.2 hm.le⟩)
        fun m _ => ⟨m, trivial, Subset.rfl⟩ }

name: Filter.Tendsto.const_mul_atTop'
description: This theorem shows that if a function tends to a limit L as x tends to infinity, then the product of a constant and the function tends to the product of the constant and L as x tends to infinity.
conditions: f(x) tends to L as x tends to infinity
conclusions: r * f(x) tends to rL as x tends to infinity
function_body:
theorem Tendsto.const_mul_atTop' (hr : 0 < r) (hf : Tendsto f l atTop) :
    Tendsto (fun x => r * f x) l atTop := by
  refine' tendsto_atTop.2 fun b => _
  obtain ⟨n : ℕ, hn : 1 ≤ n • r⟩ := Archimedean.arch 1 hr
  rw [nsmul_eq_mul'] at hn
  filter_upwards [tendsto_atTop.1 hf (n * max b 0)] with x hx
  calc
    b ≤ 1 * max b 0 := by
    { rw [one_mul]
      exact le_max_left _ _ }
    _ ≤ r * n * max b 0 := by gcongr
    _ = r * (n * max b 0) := by rw [mul_assoc]
    _ ≤ r * f x := by gcongr

name: Filter.Tendsto.atTop_mul_const'
description: A theorem that establishes the behavior of the limit of a function multiplied by a positive constant.
conditions: f(x) tends to l as x approaches ∞
r is a positive real number
conclusions: r*f(x) tends to r*l as x approaches ∞
function_body:
theorem Tendsto.atTop_mul_const' (hr : 0 < r) (hf : Tendsto f l atTop) :
  Tendsto (fun x => f x * r) l atTop := by
  refine' tendsto_atTop.2 fun b => _
  obtain ⟨n : ℕ, hn : 1 ≤ n • r⟩ := Archimedean.arch 1 hr
  have hn' : 1 ≤ (n : R) * r := by rwa [nsmul_eq_mul] at hn
  filter_upwards [tendsto_atTop.1 hf (max b 0 * n)] with x hx
  calc
    b ≤ max b 0 * 1 := by
    { rw [mul_one]
      exact le_max_left _ _ }
    _ ≤ max b 0 * (n * r) := by gcongr
    _ = max b 0 * n * r := by rw [mul_assoc]
    _ ≤ f x * r := by gcongr

name: Filter.Tendsto.atTop_mul_neg_const'
description: Given a function f(x) that tends to limit l as x tends to infinity and a negative real number r, the theorem asserts that the function r*f(x) tends to l as x tends to negative infinity.
conditions: f(x) tends to l as x tends to infinity
r is a negative real number
conclusions: r*f(x) tends to l as x tends to negative infinity
function_body: theorem Tendsto.atTop_mul_neg_const' (hr : r < 0) (hf : Tendsto f l atTop) : Tendsto (fun x => f x * r) l atBot := by simpa only [tendsto_neg_atTop_iff, mul_neg] using hf.atTop_mul_const' (neg_pos.mpr hr)

name: Filter.Tendsto.atBot_mul_const'
description: A tool to show that if a function tends to a limit as x approaches -∞, then a constant multiple of that function also tends to the same limit.
conditions: f(x) tends to l as x approaches -∞
r is a positive real number
conclusions: g(x) = r * f(x) tends to l as x approaches -∞
function_body:
theorem Tendsto.atBot_mul_const' (hr : 0 < r) (hf : Tendsto f l atBot) :
    Tendsto (fun x => f x * r) l atBot := by
  simp only [← tendsto_neg_atTop_iff, ← neg_mul] at hf ⊢
  exact hf.atTop_mul_const' hr

name: Filter.Tendsto.atBot_mul_neg_const'
description: A theorem stating that if a function f(x) tends to a limit l as x approaches negative infinity, then the function f(x) multiplied by a negative constant r will tend to the limit l * r as x approaches positive infinity.
conditions: f(x) tends to a limit l as x approaches negative infinity
r is a negative real number
conclusions: f(x) * r tends to l * r as x approaches positive infinity
function_body: theorem Tendsto.atBot_mul_neg_const' (hr : r < 0) (hf : Tendsto f l atBot) : Tendsto (fun x => f x * r) l atTop := by simpa only [mul_neg, tendsto_neg_atBot_iff] using hf.atBot_mul_const' (neg_pos.2 hr)

name: Filter.Tendsto.atTop_nsmul_const
description: This tool validates that if a sequence approaches a finite limit as the variable approaches infinity, then the sequence multiplied by a constant approaches the limit multiplied by the same constant.
conditions: The sequence f(x) approaches a finite limit l as x approaches infinity
r is a positive real number
conclusions: The sequence f(x) * r approaches l * r as x approaches infinity
function_body: theorem Tendsto.atTop_nsmul_const {f : α → ℕ} (hr : 0 < r) (hf : Tendsto f l atTop) : Tendsto (fun x => f x • r) l atTop := by refine' tendsto_atTop.mpr fun s => _ obtain ⟨n : ℕ, hn : s ≤ n • r⟩ := Archimedean.arch s hr exact (tendsto_atTop.mp hf n).mono fun a ha => hn.trans (nsmul_le_nsmul hr.le ha)

name: Filter.Tendsto.atTop_nsmul_neg_const
description: A theorem proving that, if a function f(x) tends to L at infinity and a constant r is negative, then the product of r and f(x) tends to negative infinity at infinity.
conditions: f(x) tends to L at infinity.
function_body: theorem Tendsto.atTop_nsmul_neg_const {f : α → ℕ} (hr : r < 0) (hf : Tendsto f l atTop) : Tendsto (fun x => f x • r) l atBot := by simpa using hf.atTop_nsmul_const (neg_pos.2 hr)

name: Filter.Tendsto.atTop_zsmul_const
description: Tool to prove that the limit of a scalar multiple of a function at infinity is the scalar multiple of the limit of the function.
conditions: limit of f as x approaches infinity is l
conclusions: limit of rf as x approaches infinity is rl
function_body: theorem Tendsto.atTop_zsmul_const {f : α → ℤ} (hr : 0 < r) (hf : Tendsto f l atTop) : Tendsto (fun x => f x • r) l atTop := by refine' tendsto_atTop.mpr fun s => _ obtain ⟨n : ℕ, hn : s ≤ n • r⟩ := Archimedean.arch s hr replace hn : s ≤ (n : ℤ) • r; · simpa exact (tendsto_atTop.mp hf n).mono fun a ha => hn.trans (zsmul_le_zsmul hr.le ha)

name: Filter.Tendsto.atTop_zsmul_neg_const
description: If a function f tends to a finite limit l as x tends to positive infinity, then rf tends to rl as x tends to negative infinity, where r is a negative constant.
conditions: f tends to a finite limit l as x tends to positive infinity
conclusions: rf tends to rl as x tends to negative infinity
function_body:
theorem Tendsto.atTop_zsmul_neg_const {f : α → ℤ} (hr : r < 0) (hf : Tendsto f l atTop) :
    Tendsto (fun x => f x • r) l atBot := by simpa using hf.atTop_zsmul_const (neg_pos.2 hr)

name: Filter.Tendsto.atBot_zsmul_const
description: This tool proves that if the limit of a function f as a approaches -∞ exists and r is a positive integer, then the limit of r * f as a approaches -∞ also exists and is equal to r times the limit of f as a approaches -∞.
conditions: the limit of f as a goes to -∞ exists
conclusions: the limit of r ⋅ f as a goes to -∞ exists and is equal to r times the limit of f as a goes to -∞
function_body: theorem Tendsto.atBot_zsmul_const {f : α → ℤ} (hr : 0 < r) (hf : Tendsto f l atBot) : Tendsto (fun x => f x • r) l atBot := by simp only [← tendsto_neg_atTop_iff, ← neg_zsmul] at hf ⊢ exact hf.atTop_zsmul_const hr

name: Filter.Tendsto.atBot_zsmul_neg_const
description: This tool verifies the behavior of a function that tends to a limit as x tends to negative infinity when multiplied by a negative constant.
conditions: f tends to l as x tends to negative infinity
conclusions: (λ x. f(x) • r) tends to l as x tends to positive infinity
function_body:
theorem Tendsto.atBot_zsmul_neg_const {f : α → ℤ} (hr : r < 0) (hf : Tendsto f l atBot) :
    Tendsto (fun x => f x • r) l atTop := by simpa using hf.atBot_zsmul_const (neg_pos.2 hr)

name: isUpperSet_empty
description: A tool to verify that the empty set is an upper set, meaning there are no elements to violate the condition of being an upper set.
conditions: The given set is the empty set (∅).
conclusions: The empty set is an upper set.
function_body: theorem isUpperSet_empty : IsUpperSet (∅ : Set α) := fun _ _ _ => id

name: isLowerSet_empty
description: A tool that proves the empty set is a lower set.
conclusions: The empty set is a lower set.
function_body: theorem isLowerSet_empty : IsLowerSet (∅ : Set α) := fun _ _ _ => id

name: isUpperSet_univ
description: This tool checks that the universal set is an upper set, meaning it contains all elements of any subset.
conditions: The universal set contains all elements of the set.
conclusions: The universal set is an upper set for any subset.
function_body: theorem isUpperSet_univ : IsUpperSet (univ : Set α) := fun _ _ _ => id

name: isLowerSet_univ
description: A tool to prove that the universal set (the set of all elements) is a lower set.
conditions: a is an element of the universal set
